How I saved $4,200 traveling for 3 weeks in Portugal and wasn't living like a caveman. 
 My Portugal trip in January should have cost me about $6,800 to start. I ended up spending about $2,600 in total. Here's how. 
 
Flights: $1,850 saved
 I had 68,000 Chase Sapphire Preferred points plus a bunch of United miles accumulated by company travel in the last 2 years. I see in mid September that there is a bonus transfer to United, with Chase giving 25% more points when you transfer. This is now enough points for a saver-level round trip from Newark to Lisbon. It costs $121 in taxes/fees. The ticket was $982 in February (my travel month). 
 But I timed it right. I left 1/9 and got back 1/30. Mid-winter fares post-holidays are very cheap to Europe from NE. If I had wanted to go in June, it was over $1,400 for the same dates. 
 
Lodging: $1,600 saved
 3 weeks split between Lisbon (8 nights), Porto (6 nights) and Lagos, Algarve (7 nights). I didn't stay in hotels, but apartments through Booking.com. I did this in January, peak off-season. Owners want any bookings. For example, my one-bedroom apt in Lisbon (Alfama) was $54/night. If I wanted that in June, it would be $150. 
 In Lagos, I got a guesthouse room. Ocean view. $47/night (includes breakfast). This is also a credit card portal booking. That is, via Chase travel portal using my Sapphire card. Effectively I got another 5% back in points. 
 
Other stuff: $750+ saved
 Museum stuff. Lisbon Card €42 for 72 hours. That included entry to Jeronimos Monastery, Belem Tower, transit, etc. About €60 total value. 
 Off season tours. Like Porto to Douro valley wine tour. In summer it's €85. I did it in off season for €55. Also, only 6 of us instead of a packed van. 
 Eating. No reservations required at Taberna da Rua das Flores in Lisbon in January. I just walked in on a Tuesday. Same meal, no tourist tax. 
 
Tradeoffs (sorry)
 It rained 4 days in Porto. Some beach restaurants closed in Lagos. Shorter days. Sun sets around 5:30pm. But hey, Portugal in Jan had it hitting 60F most days in Lisbon in the afternoon. And I had almost no one with me at Pena Palace in Sintra (on a Wed. morning). That's 2 hour line in summer. 
 
So... 
 Flights: $1,850 saved
 Lodging: $1,600
 Tours and attractions: $750
 Total: $4,200 saved. Enough for my next trip (already planning). Greece in November?

Garage now permanently smells of PB Blaster. Grabbed the bike Aug. 2nd. Guy in Hillsboro (Russ) had it tarp'ed up since 2011. '78 Honda CB750K. 31,400 miles. Covered in dust (matte finish). $1400 cash. Odo cable seized. Carb's solid-varnished. Some critter's family was living in the airbox. You know...first-owner-in-10-years thing. 
 First week: degrease everything. 4 cans Simple Green. 1 entire Saturday spent degreasing 11 years of grimey gunk off engine cases just to see what I'm working with. Eng. cases are good. No cracks. No stripped threads. Just cosmetic corrosion on fin edges. 
 Second week: ripped out carb bank (bank of 4, Keihin CV carbs). Dunked in Berrymans' Dip for 3 days. Rebuilt with CB750 Supply kit. $89. For all 4 sets of gaskets, O-rings and float valves. Most satisfying afternoon thus far. Watching float bowls that were dried-up-scrusted open up again. 
 So far, I'm tracking on a note-book in the work bench: 
 bike: $1400 
 carb kit: $89 
 Battery (YB9-B, old thing was like a brick): $34 
 new fuel lines/inline filter: $22 
 degreaser/brushes/gloves/shop towels: ~ $60 
 NGK plugs (x4): $18 
 Total: $1623 as of tonight (Sep. 20th). 
 Comp. check: 145, 148, 142, 140 psi (4 cylinders). Winning the lottery w/ 48-yr. air cooled engine. Haven't tried starting yet. Next weekend. New fuel in tank. Points gapped. Neighbor Dave (rebuilt 2 of these himself) keepin' me calm about not-rushing-first-kick. Uh...I'm-a-rush-it.

blog_personal_04_luna.text:
January 8, 2025.  51 years old.  Time to tie up those running shoes.  Just gotta get to the end of my first half marathon after having a knee replacement. 

A year ago this would have been absurd.  In March 2024, I had my right knee replaced.  Years of arthritis made stairs, long walks, and even exiting my car a living hell.  The recovery was long, and embarrassing.  My physical therapist, Elena Morales, had me walking 5 minutes around my neighborhood in Sacramento, CA.  By June, I was walking 2 miles without stopping.  September had me on the stationary bike and doing strength workouts 3x a week. 

I never considered running.  Then my friend Marcus told me about the Davis Turkey Trot Half Marathon coming up November 27, 2025.  "You don't have to run the entire way.  You just need to train consistently."

So I started.  Walk-run 1 min jog / 2 min walk for 20 minutes.  My first workout: 1.4 miles.  My knee was swollen.  Ice on it.  Phone call to Elena.  Lesson learned: progress doesn't mean painful. 

I now workout 4x a week.  Easy walk-runs on Tues.  Strength workouts on Thurs.  Long, slow Saturday runs.  Sunday is stretch and recovery.  Long distance only increases by 1/2 mile at most per week.  In February, I did 3 miles.  April: 6 miles.  I just did 9 miles on Saturday at the American River Parkway.  2 hrs 11 minutes. 

No personal record setting here.  Just gotta get to the end in Davis before they close the course.  Ideally, I'll finish with a smile and be able to walk.  I know I'll be moving much slower than I did at 30.  (mostly because I didn't run at 30.)  But every mile is a reminder that my body is still a surprise. 

51 years old.  Titanium knee.  Extremely forgiving training regimen.  I'm finding out that starting again can be an accomplishment too.

January 8, 2025. I put on my running shoes, ready to race. My age? 51. The challenge? Completing my first half marathon since my knee replacement surgery.

A year ago, this would have seemed absurd. In March 2024, I had my right knee replaced. Arthritis had been making stairs, extended walking and even exiting the car a painful experience. My recovery was gradual and humbling. My physical therapist, Elena Morales, had me walk for 5 minutes at a time in my Sacramento, CA neighborhood. By June, I could walk 2 miles without stopping. In September, I was working out on a stationary bike and doing weight lifting exercises 3 days per week.

Running seemed out of the question. Until my friend, Marcus, told me about the Davis Turkey Trot Half Marathon. It's taking place November 27, 2025. "You don't have to run the entire thing," Marcus said. "Just be consistent."

So I started with walk/runs. A minute jogging and then 2 minutes walking. For 20 minutes total. My first session was 1.4 miles. And my knee swelled after the workout. I applied ice. I phoned Elena. "Remember, progress isn't the same as pain," she told me.

Now I work out 4 days per week. On Tuesday, I do a light walk/run. On Thursday, weightlifting. On Saturday, I do a longer slower walk/run. And on Sunday, I stretch and recover. I only add half a mile of distance each week to my long walks. Last month, I did 3 miles in February. In April, I worked up to 6. Last Saturday, I managed 9 miles on the American River Parkway in Davis. It took me 2 hours and 11 minutes.

I'm not trying to set a personal best. I just want to make it across the finish line in Davis before they shut the race down. If I can do it with a smile on my face and with the ability to walk afterwards, even better. My pace is going to be slower now than when I was 30. (No running at 30 for me.) But each mile makes me feel like my body is capable of surprising me.

At 51, with a titanium knee and an incredibly patient training schedule, I'm discovering that the new beginning can be a form of winning.

blog_personal_06_glm.text:
Time zone co-parenting: schooling from Berlin and Toronto

When Marcus started teaching at Humboldt University in September 2023, we knew our co-parenting setup was going to get interesting. Marcus moved to Berlin. I stayed in Toronto with our two kids, Elena (11) and Theo (8). A six hour time difference isn’t that bad, right? Except when it comes to parent-teacher night.

Eighteen months in. This is what we’ve got.

The calendar. It’s like a holy text. Everything in Google Calendar. School stuff. Swimming at Wallace Emerson Community Centre. Theo’s Wednesday 4pm EST speech therapy sessions. No calendar. It didn’t happen. Marcus looks at it every morning. 7am Berlin. 1am Toronto time for me. So he gets my last-night events before I’m even awake.

Shifting participation. He can’t physically be in the gym at Earl Grey Public School. But he’s on video for parent-teacher interviews. Often 8pm or 9pm his time. Elena’s teachers have been great at getting early times. Where it’s really body-in-the-room stuff—the winter concert, pick-up for March break—he flies in. He’s been back four times now. Staying in a rental near us on Dovercourt Road.

Tuesdays and Fridays are “Berlin dinner.” 2:30pm for Marcus. So he has lunch, they have dinner. We talk about the week. Theo likes to demo his LEGO creations on the camera. Elena mostly eye-rolls through it, but she’s always there. We keep it sacred. We don’t book playdates for that time.

Things suck sometimes. Like last February when Theo had the flu. I was up all night. Marcus was 6600km away. Felt useless. But we’ve learned there’s stuff he can do. All the online stuff. Ordering school supplies. Scheduling Theo’s therapy sessions. Looking into March break camps. From Berlin. The practical help is helpful.

Kids are weirdly good at time zone math. Theo can do Toronto → Berlin in his head faster than I can. And then there’s daylight savings. Europe does it two weeks earlier than North America (spring). So we have a two-week period where the difference is five hours. Everyone gets confused.

This isn’t the co-parenting we thought we’d be doing. When we split up in 2021. But when Elena was with her school counselor recently, she said she had “a dad in two countries.” She said it like it was a superpower. Okay then.

If you’re doing this: calendar. Sacred time for calls. And split up the invisible work. Continentally. It’s not perfect, but it’s ours.

Clocked out from my last shift at St. Luke's MC a Tuesday in July 2024 and started the UX bootcamp Monday of the following week. Now three weeks into a product design position at a healthtech startup in Providence. 14 months later. 
 I want to document what it's been like because the timeline I thought it would follow was not the timeline it followed. 

Months 1-3 was GA part time UX/UI course while working 3 12hr shifts at night a week at hospital. Would leave at 7am from work, sleep till 1pm then hop on for 3pm cohort Zoom call. Two projects from that timeframe, one was a redesign of my hospital's own patient discharge instructions (turns out it's shitty ass paperwork. It's bad. Look at it. You're a designer, not a nurse giving it out.). 
 The other was a medication reminder app. Dosewise. 
 
 Months 4-7 rough middle ground here. 
 November 2024 quit nursing all together (had saved 8 months expense for this). This time was all informational interviews. Did 34 (tracked in spreadsheet). Mostly from a Providence UX meetup called Ocean State UX. Meets 2nd Thursday of the month. Coworking space on Westminster st. 
 11 portfolio feedback calls from those. 
 
 8-10 months, 3rd case study. (unsolicited). Redesigning nurse shift handoff tool at my old hospital. Interviewed 6 former coworkers about the places where information is lost between shifts. This one got the most calls back than both others. This one was the one where my nursing expertise was the point. Not needing to explain it away. 
 
 11-14: 61 apps, 9 first interviews. 3 final interviews. 1 offer. 
 Offer was from Verve Health (40 people) for tools for home health aides. Sept 2 2025.  $89k starting salary. (roughly 6k less than my last year of nursing with diffs. No more nights)
 
 If you are starting now. Be prepared for months 5-7 to feel like nothing. But it's not nothing. It's compound interviews.

 Months 8-10: I did a 3rd case study on my own. An unsolicited redesign for shift handoff for the nurses at my previous hospital.  If you're just starting now, I would recommend setting up your plan to expect months 5 - 7 to feel like nothing is happening. It's not. It's the compound of the interviews.

blog_personal_10_luna.text:
We started homeschooling our son (Eli) in September 2022 at the age of 8 reading on about a 1st grade level. Dyslexia made any worksheet feel like a test he'd already failed. He could draw a pretty picture to explain the water cycle, but reading a short paragraph about the water cycle was tiring and frustrating and humiliating. 
 Over the first year we tried three popular LA curriculums. One was really into independent reading. Another went through spelling lists too quickly. We didn't stay with either of them for longer than 6 weeks. We settled on All About Reading level 2 + All About Spelling. Short 20min lessons. Super explicit about phonograms, syllables, blending. Letter tiles and tapping out sounds on the table. Reading decodable books rather than guessing at a picture. By February 2023 he could read simple chapter books out loud without wanting to curl up in a ball and hide. 
 We did Institute for Excellence in Writing (Primary Arts of Language) for writing. I liked that they kept the physical writing and the idea/brain work separate. He would dictate his responses to me and I would type them first. Then he'd copy one sentence or two sentences and then finally write some short paragraphs. His favorite was a story retelling of 'The Three Little Pigs' from the perspective of the wolf. 
 Math was not as bad, but word problems were hard. Reading was getting in the way of demonstrating understanding. Math-U-See was good because it was hands-on and consistent. We spent almost two months doing multiplication with pretty blocks before we did the written equations. I would read all the word problems aloud. He could draw the problem or verbally explain. 
 The big shift was in slowing down. 3ish focused hours of school each morning with 25min movement breaks. Also, not comparing with the school down the road. In May 2024, Eli finished reading an entire 120pg adventure book on his own. It took him almost 3 weeks. But he finished and wanted to know when we were going to read the next one. 
 Eli still has dyslexia. Homeschooling is not easy breezy. But we found curriculums that gave Eli tools without the pressure. But more importantly it gave him a sense of being able to do it.

My son Eli started homeschooling in Sept 2022, he was 8yo and reading at about a 1st grade level. He has dyslexia so it felt like every worksheet was a test he was already failing. He could explain the water cycle, and draw a detailed picture, but reading a paragraph about it was just so overwhelming and embarrassing. 
 Our first year we went through 3 popular language arts programs. One was very reader heavy, another rushed through the spelling list, neither of them worked more than 6 weeks. We ended up using All About Reading Level 2 and All About Spelling. It was so quick and easy, 20 min a day. Super explicit with phonograms, syllables, blending. He had letter tiles and sounds on table to tap and was reading decodable books instead of just guessing from pictures. By Feb 2023 Eli was reading simple chapter books out loud without shutting down. 
 For writing we used the Primary Arts of Language (Institute for Excellence in Writing). I loved that it helped separate the mechanics of writing from ideation. First we dictated (I wrote what he said) or at least that is what he'd dictate to me. Then it was 1 sentence, then 2, then short paragraphs. One of his favorite assignments was re-telling "The Three Little Pigs" but from the wolf's perspective. 
 Math was a little easier but word problems were a challenge because reading caused a roadblock to demonstrating understanding. Math-U-See was great because it was hands-on and predictable. Multiplication took us almost 2 months with colorful blocks before we transitioned to the written math equations. I'd read all the word problems aloud and he could either draw out the problem or verbally talk through it. 
 The big shift was slowing down. We school about 3 really focused hours in the morning and do movement breaks every 25 min or so. Another thing was to stop comparing ourselves to the local school calendar. My son read a whole 120 page adventure book (by himself) in May 2024. Took him almost 3 weeks, but he got it done. Then he wanted to read the sequel right away. 
 It's not like we've cured his dyslexia or that now it's all a piece of cake. But with the right curricula it gave Eli the tools without the pressure. More importantly, it helped him believe in himself.

blog_personal_12_glm.text:
My mom hit 65 last June. Instead of a birthday celebration, she wanted to do something even cooler. Let's walk the TMB together for 11 days. Not the whole 170 km. She made that clear from day one. We'll stick to the classic part of the French and Italian TMB. We'll cut a few stages where we'll take the bus. And we'll keep pace under 12 km a day, rather than the normal 20+ km. It was the best decision. 
 A lot of the forums for the TMB have ultralight aficionados, and people talking about getting up at 5 am to walk. Listen to them, but not too much. 
 Here's what worked for us: 
 Packing. 
 Mom: 7 kg. Me: 10 kg (includes shared 1st aid kit and all that wine we kept purchasing in Courmayeur) 
 She packed in 1 single 40L.  Had 2 x merino shirts for hiking.  1 x convertible pants.  Rain jacket.  Down jacket.  No way out: she brought her trekking poles. She got a knee replacement in 2021. She said the poles made her legs feel like they gained 5 years. I overpacked the heck out of shirts. Had to send 1/2 back from Chamonix. 
 Pacing. 
 Rule: no more than one major climb per day. Done. 
 The climb from Les Contamines to Col du Bonhomme (2329 m) almost did us in on day 3. After that, we reconfigured everything. Leave by 8:30. Have lunch around noon in refuge. Order tartiflette. Always. Stop walking by 3:30 pm. This gives mom 1 full hour to stretch out and shower before aperitif. July books out for many of the refuges (Refuge Nant Borrant, Rifugio Bonatti) for months. Book in March. 
 Truth. 
 She cried at the viewpoint at Fenetre d' Arpette.  I kinda did too. 
 There were 2 days where she took the bus, I walked (Les Chapieux to Courmayeur. No regrets. She had espresso in the town. I trudged through Col de La Seigne in the rain). 
 Pace is not bad. It's how we did this. 
 If you're thinking about doing this with your parent, get the "flexible" versions of everything. 
 And bring cards. Because refuge nights are long. And mom destroyed me at gin rummy every night. 
 Would I do it again? We've put in the Walker's Haute route for her 70th. She says she'll train this time. She won't. All good.

Last June, my mom hit 65. No birthday party. She wanted something better. She wanted to do the Tour du Mont Blanc with me for 11 days. (But not the full 170 km. That was her opening salvo.) We would do the standard French and Italian sections. Miss a few with bus sections. Average out to around 12km/day rather than the 20+.etc. Best decision ever. 
 Biggest thing that you'll see online for the TMB. All the ulta-light and 5am folks. Dismiss. For what it's worth - 
 > Packing: 
 Mom packed 7kg, I packed 10kg (with the group first aid kit + the amount of wine we were buying in courm). 
 For Mom: 
  - 1x 40l backpack 
  - 2x merino hiking t-shirts 
  - 1x convertible pants 
  - 1x rain-shell 
  - 1x down jacket 
  - And, importantly her own hiking poles. She had a knee replacement in 2021. Said the poles give her 5 years back on her legs. 
 I packed far too many shirts. Ended up sending half of them home from Chamonix. 
 > Pacing: 
 Set ourselves a limit to 1 large climb per day max. After that, stop. That nearly killed us with the climb from les contamines to col du bonhomme (2329m) on day 3. So, we changed things after that. Leave by 8:30ish. Have lunch at a refuge midday. (Make sure to get tartiflette. Every time.) Done walking by 3:30 so that mom had an hour to stretch and shower before apéro. Things to consider, some refuges like Refuge Nant Borrant, or Rifugio Bonatti are booked out months in advance for july. Book in march. 
 > Real talk: 
 Yup. She cried at the view point at fenetre d'arpet. So did I. Also, there were two days where she hopped the bus and I went on foot. (Les chapieux to Courm, no regrets. She had espresso in town. Meanwhile I was hiking col de la seigne in the rain.) So pace isn't giving up. It's what made the trip possible in the first place. 
 If you're going to do this with your old parent. Book the "flexible" options for everything. 
 Take a pack of cards. The evenings at the refuge are long. And, Mom beat the crap out of me at gin rummy every night. 
 Would I do it again? We've scheduled the Walker's Haute Route for her 70th already. Said she'll be training this time. Nah, she won't. No worries.

i took a wild chance on a six week intro to wheel class at Clayworks on Fulton St. Two days after my 38th birthday. It was a joke b-day gift from my husband. I never thought I'd be there 14 months later.

first time I centered a bowl it took 40 minutes. It looked like a beret. My instructor, a gentle dude named Marcus. He's been throwing for 20 years. Said 90% of the battle is centering. Nobody figures it out the first week. He was being nice. I didn't figure it out until week 9.

The first four months of my work was just all leaning shit. i have an October mug that leans so hard, it looks like it's pouring even when it's not. I kept it on my desk as a reminder. Didn't throw it away. My wife started calling my early stuff 'the Leaning Tower of Ceramics'.

In February on a Tuesday night class I threw a set of four cereal bowls. They actually matched. Same height. Same wall thickness. Walls so thin, you could see the light through the greenware. Dear Professor Martinez,

Regarding my economics term paper titled "The Impact of Minimum Wage Changes on Part-Time Employment in California (2012 - 2023)", I would like to make sure how I should interpret the results from the regression in Q3.

In my model, I find that a 10% increase in real minimum wage leads to a 0.8% decrease in part-time employment (coefficient: -0.080, p = 0.03), adjusted for county fixed effect, year fixed effect, unemployment, and industry composition. Meanwhile, in Freakley (2021), it says there was not any statistically significant employment decrease after minimum wage increases. I currently mention in my paper that my result is "consistent with a small negative impact on employment", but I'm worried this might be inconsistent with the source.

Should I talk about this as being inconsistent, or is it more the case that there are data and method differences leading to this? The Freakley paper is based on national quarterly data from 1990 - 2018, whereas I'm working with annual county-level data in California from 2012 - 2023, with a particular focus on part-time employees. If I remove 2020 - 2021 from the data, the coefficient is no longer statistically significant. This may be due to the effects of the pandemic on the labor market.

Do you suggest I modify my discussion to highlight the caveats and not go so far as to say it's inconsistent with Freakley?

Best,
Jordan Lee

essay_opinion_01_luna.text:
Before 2030, Times Square should be free of cars. Not as a gimmick. As the logical extension to New York's decades-long endeavor to reclaim public spaces.

It’s happening now. In 2009 Mayor Michael Bloomberg closed traffic on Broadway through Times Square and set up temporary pedestrian plazas from 42nd to 47th Streets. It seemed radical, but it quickly felt normal. The pedestrian plazas limited vehicular conflicts, allowed for more pedestrian activity, offered places for tables, performances, and a place to stand in one of the busiest places on the planet.

But Times Square is a confusing place—a sensory overload designed to knock you over with its bright lights and flashy ads. Millions visit every year. And still cars and trucks thread through. Three-hundred-thousand pedestrians per day walk there. Sidestepping barricades, delivery trucks, taxis, buses, right turning traffic. All while their eyes are on the advertisements telling them all the possibilities New York has to offer.

A permanent car-free Times Square doesn’t mean never cars. Emergency services. Maintenance. Access. Even certain delivery schedules could continue to access the area. Private vehicles, however, and standard through traffic should be eliminated. Essential travel is there for Seventh, Sixth, and Eighth Avenues. Let the central square be a civic space and not just a pedestrian oasis cut off by the presence of machines.

It's not just about aesthetics. Better air quality. Fewer accidents. Less noise. Safer crossing. Important in a city where we have children, elders, workers, visitors, all jockeying for space. Also Times Square is one of the few places on the planet that has the potency to communicate a message. New York values people more than quick travel through Midtown.

In 2030 we should finish what we started in 2009. First and foremost Times Square should be for the people who walk there, work there, perform there, and bring it to life. There’s plenty of roads for cars to drive on. Let one square take a breath.

Car-free Times Square by 2030 isn't just a stunt. It's the logical evolution of the decades-long experiment of bringing back public space in New York City.

As far back as 2009, New York City (during the Bloomberg mayoralty) closed Broadway through Times Square to cars, and created temporary pedestrian plazas between 42nd and 47th Streets. The interventions felt revolutionary then, but they quickly became normal. They de-conflicted with cars. They allowed people to spread out. They provided space for tables, performances, and the pleasure of standing still in the busiest area on earth.

But Times Square is weird. It's meant to shock the senses. It's the place where millions of people congregate every year. And yet cars and trucks still criss-cross in the middle of it all. Over 300,000 pedestrians flow through the space every day. They weave in and out of barricades, deliveries, taxis, buses, and turning cars. All while gazing up at ads that promise the world from the city that never sleeps.

If Times Square were permanently car-free, it doesn't mean all cars would be forbidden. Emergency services, maintenance crews, accessibility, and scheduled deliveries could still come and go. But private vehicles and through traffic could be eliminated. Critical movement could flow in the surrounding avenues (Seventh, Sixth, Eighth), but the main plaza would turn into a public space. Not a pedestrian island amid the clanking machines.

It's not just an aesthetic preference. Cleaner air. Fewer crashes. Less noise. Safer crossings. It's good stuff in a city of kids, elders, workers, and tourists all jockeying for the same limited space. And Times Square is one of those few places on the planet that has the symbolic importance to make a statement. To say New York City places people over the convenience of driving through Midtown.

Finish what you started in 2009 by 2030. Times Square should be for the people that walk through it. The ones that work there and perform there. The ones that help make it a living thing. Let the cars have all the other roads. Let one square breathe.

essay_opinion_03_glm.text:
I found that letter in March. Hidden inside a copy of Joan Didion’s The White Album that my mom had sent me in 2019. Three pages. Handwritten. Dated October 14. That year. The neighbor's dog, the tomato prices on Saturday in Davis California. How I was not getting enough sleep in my Brooklyn apartment. Her pretty forward-leaning handwritten script. I’d clearly read it at a glance. And texted back a thumbs-up.

God that thumbs-up has been haunting me.

I’m no nostalgia-monger. I love iMessage. I sent 47 texts yesterday. Mostly jokes. Mostly great. The immediacy of digital communication is a miracle. Don't wanna give it up. But I think we've lost sight of the role the handwritten letter plays. And in doing so we've silently given it up.

You see here's the thing about a letter. It's an expensive thing for someone to send. My mom probably spent 40 minutes writing those three pages. Time is the only thing you can't return or regift. You see it with handwriting. Because every slightly crammed line close to the margin. It's saying I went ahead anyway. With a text. It's saying I thought about you for 4 seconds. Sometimes that's enough. But not always enough.

Then there's the materiality of the letter. That letter was in an envelope. Going through sorting centers. Crossing the country. Dropped in the blue mailbox on Fifth Ave. Went to my apartment. My mom's hand was holding the actual paper. I read that letter again when she passed in June last. It almost felt like I could feel the force of the pen. Show me the emoji for that.

So I began writing back before it was too late for my mom. And since then. I've written back. To my friend Dana in Portland. To my old prof in Chicago. A page a month max. That's the point. The content restriction. Can't just write a paragraph about the neighbor's dog with your hand. Because it'll matter. Your wrist will tell you you've said enough. Your heart, forced to slow down to the pace of the pen, has things to say that your thumb won't.

We don't need words. We need slowness. The letter is slowness you can hold.

 I'd read through it once and given her a thumbs up, apparently, via text. 
 Since then I've been haunted by the thumbs up. 

I'm not a nostalgia guy.  I love iMessage.  Sent 47 texts yesterday, mostly jokes.  Mostly good jokes.  The rapidity of digital communication is a miracle.  I wouldn't give it up.  But I think we've given up a piece of real estate in stealth.  A piece of real estate that nothing else can touch. 
 The piece of real estate occupied by the handwritten letter. 
 A letter costs something.  It costs the sender.  My mom may have spent 40 minutes on those three pages.  Time can't be returned or regifted.  Handwriting is the signifier.  All the slightly cramped lines on the edges of the page.  I kept going.  It says.  A text message.  I thought about you for 4 seconds.  That's fine sometimes.  It isn't always enough. 

And there's the reality.  It was put in an envelope.  It went through sorting centers.  Crossed the country.  Went in a blue mailbox on 5th Ave.  Made its way to my apartment.  My mom's actual hand was holding actual paper.  When she passed last June I reread it and could almost feel the force of the pen.  Show me the emoji for that.

And your heart.  Slowed by the speed of the pen.  Speaks things the thumb never would.

essay_opinion_07_luna.text:
Why every city should take a page from Bogotá's Ciclovía Sundays (not as a novelty but a civic fantasy to do every week)

In Bogotá, on Sundays and public holidays, for seven hours, between 7am and 2pm, around 140km of streets are blocked to cars. Avenues that are usually for vehicles are open to cyclists, joggers, skaters, parents and their children with strollers, old people walking. The practice started December 15, 1974, when a small group of citizens staged a protest and blocked a few streets in the city center. This Sunday, 50 years later, more than a million people might use the network in a given week.

The genius of the Ciclovía is that it doesn't need much. Not a new subway line, or a new stadium, or a cutting-edge fleet of electric buses. Just barriers, traffic wardens, public bathrooms, first-aid tents. And the gumption to say: for seven hours, let us care more about moving and feeling than parking.

I remember seeing for the first time a video of Bogotá's Carrera Séptima on a Sunday. It didn't feel like an avenue; it felt like a living room. Kids on wobbly bicycles, teenagers on their tricks, grandpas and grandmas holding hands, juice-sellers and arepas. No new park. Just the one they had already. The street.

It's a big difference. Most urban policies focus on travel. How fast can workers arrive downtown? How many cars can squeeze at a given intersection? How smoothly can cargo be shipped? The Ciclovía is a space for something else. For being in the city, without having to consume anything or go anywhere.

Some will say: street closures create disorder. Well, yes. Cities are about conflict. Not about pretending that the only valid way to occupy public space is to drive a car. A Sunday closure is also a harmless way to try things out. To feel what a calmer, safer street is like before we even discuss whether and how to reconfigure it.

Why not start in every city? One avenue. Four hours. One Sunday every month. See what happens. People will show up. Not because they are ordered to get fit. But because they're invited to feel like they belong.

Let every city do Bogotá's Ciclovía Sundays—not as a novelty, but as a weekly cultural act of imagination.

In Bogotá, every Sunday and public holiday, from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m., about 140 kilometers of roads are closed to cars. Bicycle riders, joggers, skaters, stroller-pushing families, slow-walking old folks; they fill the thoroughfares that are normally the domain of cars. It started on Dec. 15, 1974, when a small citizens' initiative blocked off a few downtown roads. Today, half a century later, more than a million people might use the system in a week.

What's so brilliant about Ciclovía? It doesn't ask for much. No new subway line. No new stadium. No futuristic fleet of electric buses. Just some barricades and some traffic cops. Public restrooms. A few first-aid stations. The political will to say: For seven hours, our priority is motion and enjoyment over parking.

When I first saw videos of what Bogotá's Carrera Séptima became on Sunday, my reaction was this: The thoroughfare was no longer a transportation artery. It felt like a common room. There were kids struggling to ride bikes. There were teens showing off. There were grandmas holding hands. There were juice and arepa vendors. Bogotá hadn't added a new park. It had simply opened the existing one—the street—to its citizens.

It's an important difference. So much of what we do in cities revolves around commuting. How can we make it faster for people to get downtown? How can we increase the number of cars through an intersection? How can we optimize the flow of goods? But Ciclovía adds one thing: the ability to be in a city for the sake of being there. Not because you have to shop or because you need to go somewhere.

Detractors will say it's too disruptive to close off streets. And yes, it is. That's the point of cities. They're supposed to mediate between different needs. They're not supposed to act as if cars are the only valid inhabitants of public spaces. And Sunday's is an experiment that's relatively risk-free. It allows citizens to experience what a less noisy, less dangerous street would be like, before any debates arise around what it might look like permanently.

Every city could start with something modest: one thoroughfare, four hours, once a month on Sundays. And then see what happens. People will show up. Not because they're being told they should be exercising. But because they're being invited to be part of it.

The Met has been my home since I was 9 when my grandmother pulled out two dollars and we wandered the Egyptian wing all day. That's what the Met was. A place where, if you were a girl from Queens, you could gaze upon a Temple of Dendur and see the whole world's history as your own.

But now, even that's expensive. The Met, in August 2022, went from $25 in mandatory entry to $30 for out of state. And then $35 in 2025 - some of the highest priced tickets in any museum in America. You could "pay what you want" in theory if you're a NY'er. But this offer is buried in a morass of legalese. The kiosks are now showing full price first. You have to know the trick even exists. You have to be comfortable saying to a Met worker that you want to give them a dollar. For a family of 4 from the Bronx, it's not a discount, it's casting.

Met leaders justify these price increases as simple: post pandemic costs. Insurance. Climate control for 2M items. Sure. The Met's endowment isn't what it used to be. But let's talk about who they're asking to cover it. Not the people socializing at the gala dinners. Not the tourists. $35 is chump change on a $600 hotel room for a night. It's the kids from Newark on the tour buses. The nanny with the day off. The art school student that used to come draw on Tuesdays.

A city is defined by the access you can give your least well off. You have Central Park. Free. Staten Island Ferry. Free. The Met was going to be one of those public places. Public land. A lease with the city. Funded by public money in some respects. $35 at the door says something else. Culture is a commodity. You are a customer.

Here's the solution. Easy. The British Museum and Tate in London have stayed free of charge through worse financial climates than now. Because England said: No. This is a must have. The Met could go that route. Go for it. Find the endowments. Get the city involved. And stop quietly pushing out the people this is for.

Or else one day soon there'll be a 9 year old from Queens looking up at the steps on 5th Ave. Her grandmother will see the price and keep on going. And the Met will be less for it. So will the city.

My 9-year old daughter, Maya, got a flip phone for her birthday in March. No smartphone.

It's a scratched-up purple plastic-bodied Nokia. With a tiny screen. And a battery that won't die. She calls me to let me know when soccer practice is over early at Lincoln Elementary. She texts her grandma in Sacramento. She calls to say hi when she's walking the 3 blocks from our apartment to the library on Saturdays. That's pretty much it.

This isn't anti-technology. Maya's got plenty of technology in her life. A school Chromebook. Science videos. How to ask Alexa for the weather. But there's a specific kind of technology—the kind that comes with a smartphone. The constant notifications. The video. The games. The advertising. The social comparisons. The adult engagement. That's what I want to delay.

Maya's 9. So she's still figuring out how to be bored. She stares out the bus window on the way to swim lessons. Sees the mural on 14th Street. The guy with the oranges near the station. Is there a moon between the buildings? Last week she spent 20 minutes trying to figure out how to do a magic card trick. She had nothing else to do. I don't want to take up all the gaps. Before she finds out what might grow in the gaps.

Plus, a flip phone encourages intentional communication. If Maya calls me, she's got something to say. If I call Maya, she says "Hi, Dad". Instead of looking at a screen while she's in the middle of playing a game. We have this family rule to keep phones in backpacks while we eat. By 7:30pm her phone is often off. No group chat to moderate. No social media to keep an eye on. No need to explain why some kid's vacation video has 400 likes.

Obviously, a flip phone is annoying. She can't really share pictures. Or use maps. Or the messaging app everyone else in her class is using. She'll sometimes grumble about being the only 4th grader who doesn't have an iPhone. I tell her "not yet" is a full answer.

Eventually, she'll get a smartphone. But for now, I want her first phone to be a tool of independence. Not a handheld internet.

I remember paying $14.99 for my first CD. Tower records on Sunset blvd. April 2003. It was Radiohead’s ‘Hail To The Thief’. I listened to it so many times over the summer I can still recall the seam between ‘2+2=5’ and ‘Sit Down. Stand Up’. How one track faded into another.

We lost that. Not just the money ($14.99 a lot for a 14yo). We lost the seam. We lost the transition. We lost the decision of the band. What should come after what.

We got everything with streaming. (100m+ tracks on Spotify in 2024) but that made the order moot. Once you had infinite music, the playlist was now a algorithmic one-armed bandit. Spotify’s Discover Weekly gives you 30 songs in your earhole every Monday. Apparently most people skip songs in 5-30 seconds (studies). We don’t listen to songs. We try them out. All the time. Forever.

Once upon a time, an album was a thesis. Abbey Road ends with ‘The End’. OK Computer knows the importance of where ‘Fitter Happier’ belongs as that soulless in-between ‘Karma Police’ and ‘Electioneering’. Even a mixtape (I made dozens of these painfully slow Sony double-tape machines in hs) was an artifact of love. You considered what would come after what. The order was the statement. You could read someone’s soul by the space between a Radiohead track and a Bjork track you chose to follow it up with.

Now the queue is randomized by default. ‘Enhance’ suggests songs the machine decides are right. Skip. Skip. Skip. Most Spotify users end up listening to the same 40-ish tracks every week out of this infinite library. (infinite choice made people more narrow, not more broad).

I don’t want to be nostalgic. Streaming is amazing in many ways. A kid in Fresno can listen to Fela Kuti and Fugazi in the same afternoon (free). But there was a dark side to the abundance. Music became something you didn’t commit to. Music became ambient like the weather. Songs used to be events. Now they’re atmospheric.

I’m trying to rebel a little bit. Every Friday night I listen to 1 album from start to finish. No phone. No skip. Last week it was Alvvays ‘Blue Rev’. 51 minutes felt more like listening to music than the last 6 months.

We lost the seams. But we never noticed that.

I go to the Enoch Pratt Free Library on Cathedral St in Baltimore most tuesdays. Not once has anyone asked me to purchase anything to stay.

This isn't a weird sentence. But try to spend three hours in any public space in America. Sit in a cafe. Hang out in the food court at a mall. The lobby of a hotel. How long before someone asks you what you're buying? The library is one of the last places in the US where the entrance fee is $0. The TOS is you're a person. Enoch Pratt won't ask you for your zip. The 73 branches of the LA public library won't ask about your immigration status. After a bunch of book bans Brooklyn Public Library gave out 6600 free digital library cards to teens across the country in 2022. So Texas and Florida kids could read the books the library in their towns took off the shelf.

What else is there? Maybe the park bench. Until a municipality puts in armrests that prevent you from laying down. (500+ documented cases of hostile architecture in major US cities since 2014.) If you're a member of a church, the church? The DMV. Public, sure, but not where you wanna stay put. Everything else has been surreptitiously re-metered. Malls now are where you're surveilled by the property owner's security staff. The sidewalk cafe needs you to buy a $7 espresso to get in. Even the internet - the great equalizer - now is facilitated by data brokers who sell your library-adjacent googling to advertisers. Libraries, meanwhile, are facilitated by the Library Bill of Rights adopted by the American Library Association in 1939. Which still holds that materials should not be excluded because of the origin, beliefs or views of those who create them.

This isn't a coincidence. Between 1883-1929 Andrew Carnegie paid for 1,689 library buildings in the US, on the condition that towns commit public tax dollars to keep them free forever. He knew better than most robber barons that democracy needs rooms where you don't have to pay rent for your own citizenship.

61% of Americans went to a library or a library website in the last year according to Pew's 2024 survey. More than people voted in the last midterm election. This isn't nostalgia. It's the last commons. Notice it before it goes away.

Unsung though it was, the introduction of the Ford Model A in December of 1927 dramatically pushed forward suburbanization in America during the later 1920s and 1930s. When the long-in-the-tooth Model T finally stopped being built in May of 1927, Ford closed down its facilities for six months to retool. The introduction of the new Model A on December 2, 1927 provided Americans with a new automobile that was faster, safer, and more comfortable than what came before. The Ford Model A's price points were still in the realm of affordability for a typical middle-class family ($385 for a Roadster to around $1,400 for a Town Car) while having a level of refinement that allowed for a reasonable day-to-day drive that was significantly longer. By 1931, over four million Model A's were sold. By 1930 there were over 23 million registered automobiles in the United States with a total population of around 123 million.

The world had changed. A worker no longer had to live within walking distance of his factory or streetcar. He could now easily travel ten to fifteen miles for his commute. Thanks to the top speed of the new Ford Model A of around 65 miles per hour (versus the 40 to 45 miles per hour of the Model T), commuting to the suburbs from the cities of Detroit, Chicago, Los Angeles, etc. suddenly became convenient. Real estate developers noticed. The new sprawling subdivisions in Los Angeles began springing up on new arterial roads. In the future site of Levittown, developers in Long Island and Westchester County, NY began offering homes to car owning commuters. Consumers began shopping at new roadside businesses, diners, and even early shopping center locations (e.g. Country Club Plaza in Kansas City, opened in 1923 and grew in the late 20s), which relied on customers arriving in their cars instead of by streetcar.

The Great Depression tamped down on construction after 1929, but the direction of suburbanization was clear. Of all the vehicles of its time, the Ford Model A played the greatest role in connecting the utilitarian Model T to the post-war era of mass automobility. Making reliable, comfortable car ownership a reality for millions of average families helped to alter the American Dream from a row house next to the trolley to a detached home on a suburban lot, with a driveway in the front.

In October of 1973 the Arab members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) orchestrated a production cut and an oil embargo against the US and Netherlands in retaliation for US support of Israel in the Yom Kippur War. By early 1974 the cost of a barrel of oil had nearly quadrupled from around $3 to near $12. This oil shock highlighted just how reliant the Western world had become on a commodity it could not control.

The US was itself a significant oil producer but its production peaked in 1970. In 1973 the US imported 1/3 of its oil. For Western Europe and Japan things were worse. They imported the vast majority of their oil from the Middle East and North Africa. The oil embargo had obvious and immediate consequences. There was gas rationing in the US. The rationing involved odd even license plates for days you could purchase gas. Gas stations were crowded. There was a national 55 mph speed limit put in place in early 1974 to save fuel. The effects of the oil shock and the coal miners strike in the UK forced a 3 day workweek for industry. In Japan (which imported more than 75% of its energy) there was panic buying of consumer goods. Inflation ensued. It's called the "toilet paper panic" of 1973.

The impact of the oil shock was profound and long lasting. US inflation jumped above 12% in 1974. There was a major stock market correction. The cheap energy that had enabled economic prosperity in the postwar world came to an end. There was talk of "stagflation". Stagnant growth with inflation. Something new and previously rare. Nothing seemed to be able to fix it using conventional policy tools.

But it was also a wake up call. Western nations created the International Energy Agency in 1974 to coordinate emergency stockpiles and minimize risk. France embarked on a big nuclear energy program. Japan focused on energy efficiency. Japan became a world leader in energy efficient technology. Denmark started its journey toward wind energy. So the oil shock exposed not only the West's reliance but its ability to change.

The oil embargo of 1973 is a case study in economic interdependence. A cartel of oil producing nations could, by leveraging their commodity, nearly destroy the world's richest nations almost immediately. It was a reminder that energy security is national security. This is still relevant today to foreign policy. It is the reason for the strategic petroleum reserve. It is the reason for debates about renewable energy and supply chains today. Those gas station lines in 1973 were more than an inconvenience. They were a warning the West has never really been able to ignore.

In October 1973, Arab nations in the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries responded to perceived US support of Israel in the Yom Kippur War by reducing oil output and instituting an oil embargo against the US, Netherlands, and other allies. Over the following months, the price of oil per barrel multiplied by four: from about $3 to nearly $12 by early 1974. This oil shock was a vivid reminder of the extent to which Western countries relied on a commodity they did not produce.

The United States, which was also an important oil-producing country, reached a production peak in 1970. By 1973, it was importing about a third of its oil. Western Europe and Japan were even more reliant on oil: most petroleum they consumed came from the Middle East and North Africa. The effects of the oil embargo were immediately apparent in the US: gasoline rationing, even-odd license plate rationing to dictate which days a vehicle could be filled with gas, long lines at gas stations, and a national 55 mph speed limit to preserve fuel introduced in early 1974. Britain, simultaneously hit by the oil shock and a coal miners strike, had to introduce a three-day workweek for industry. Japan, which imported more than 75 percent of its energy, suffered from panic-buying of consumer goods and inflation (known as "toilet paper panic" in 1973).

The resulting economic harm was widespread and persistent. The US saw inflation rates increase to over 12% in 1974. Stock markets plummeted. The age of cheap energy that had enabled post-war prosperity was over. Economists had to contend with a new phenomenon of "stagflation"–stagnation coupled with inflation, which had been rare and which standard economic instruments proved ineffective against.

The oil embargo, however, also prompted action. The International Energy Agency was created in 1974 to coordinate emergency stocks and lower dependency. France embarked on a major nuclear power push. Japan invested in energy efficiency, becoming a world leader in fuel-efficient technologies. Denmark started its shift to wind power. The oil embargo showed that while dependence existed, so did adaptation.

The 1973 oil embargo is a quintessential example of economic interdependence. A cartel of oil-producing nations using the commodity as political tool could, seemingly overnight, destabilize the richest countries in the world. The oil embargo showed that energy security was national security, an insight that continues to influence foreign policy– from strategic petroleum reserves to the current debate around renewable energy and supply chains. The 1973 gas station queues were not just a nuisance. They were a reminder the West has never fully shrugged off.

I remember in September 2022 as my mom went through our grocery list at the Kroger off of Elm street three times reconfiguring it before she even started to fill the cart with items. This was the month that the Bureau of Labor Statistics finally backed up what our family had been feeling for the past few weeks: Inflation was up approximately 9.1% year-over-year, the most we have seen in 40 years. It was for our family of five in a mid sized suburb of Ohio, that number that you would hear about on the evening news wasn't some distant abstract idea; it was a dollar and cents recalculation of what we could now afford to eat.

Where before 2022 my mom would spend about $180 a week at the grocery store filling two carts, by October 2022, the same grocery list had increased to nearly $240. But she had cut the list down to where she was only filling one cart. The price for eggs that used to be $1.50 for a dozen were now over $3.50 because of an Avian flu outbreak that further increased the inflationary pressures we were feeling. Milk which was $2.80 a gallon, was now nearly $4.20 a gallon. Ground beef, something that my parents usually got every Tuesday, was now a special once a week rather than 5 nights of the week. We substituted ground beef for things like lentils and canned beans which my dad began purchasing in bulk as he finally caved into getting a membership at a Sam's Club which he had resisted for years.

Small changes were made here and there to accommodate the situation. My mom started buying the Kroger brand of cereal in place of the name brands to save a little money, probably $1.20 on each box of cereal. My younger brother (12 years old at the time) stopped getting the individual bagged snacks he enjoyed for his school lunch because the cost of those snacks had almost doubled on a per unit basis. We began planting a little bit of a vegetable garden in the spring time. Tomatoes, Peppers, Zucchini. Not just for the sake of a hobby, but to also hedge our bet against the almost 8% year-over-year increase in produce prices.

What really struck me wasn't just the calculations. But how it affected our discussions. Dinner planning, something which was relatively insignificant before, was now being discussed on a Sunday evening in terms of budgeting using a calculator on the kitchen table. My parents would start comparing receipts between Kroger, Aldi, Meijer. The additional 15 minute drive to get to Aldi was worth it to them for those savings. Even if only $15/week.

Early 2023 came around and the prices seemed to have stopped going up so quickly, but they never came down. $240 worth of groceries became the new normal. Not because we were used to it. But because there was no going back. This was a lesson I learned that year. Inflation wasn't just a number. It was a slow subtle reduction in the choices you as a family had taken for granted.

 We would make subtle adjustments. My mom would go from buying name-brand cereals to Kroger brand cereals. The savings would amount to around $1.20 per box. Marketing to children under 12 is ethically dubious because of young children's tendency to confuse information with persuasion. The American Academy of Pediatrics 2020 report says that it's typically hard for children under 8 to understand advertising's intent. So they're especially susceptible to advertising for things like sweet cereal, toys, video games, and fast food. A 6-year-old might think that a cartoon character selling colorful cereal is just telling her about an interesting product, and they won't realize the company paid the cartoon character to say that in hopes of selling more.

It's a bigger ethical issue when advertising involves the use of personal data and online platforms. In 2019 Google had to pay $170M in settlements to FTC and New York Attorney General because, among other things, YouTube was accused of not getting proper parental consent for the collection of personal information from children. And, even without the data collection, the blurring of advertising with gameplay via online games can trick children into thinking that in-game rewards or an influencer video or unboxing program has something to do with play, when in fact it's just to nudge you toward buying something.

Should we outlaw *all* advertising to children? No. Children need to hear about books and educational programs, sports equipment, nutritious food. Advertisements provide jobs and competition to the businesses that need them. But we should recognize the ethical need to restrict advertising to children, because they lack the experience, financial autonomy, and critical thinking that adults have. It's wrong to engage kids in manipulative methods or undisclosed sponsorships or bogus health claims or arm-twisting their parents into it. Or to collect kids' data for targeted advertising.

Of course, there's an onus on the parents. But it's really unreasonable to put the onus of it *all* on the parents, when companies are hiring armies of psychologists and designers and data scientists to work on kids as their market. The right approach would be to ban targeted advertising to children under 12. Have some labeling standard for advertising to make it clear when something's sponsored. Restrict advertising for junk food on kids' shows. Have serious consequences for doing it wrong. The point isn't to take *away* kids' agency, it's to preserve their agency. And you need to be mindful of childhood as an important time for learning and development, and not just a profitable time for consuming. Ethical advertising should acknowledge childhood as a stage of life.

Advertising directed towards children under the age of 12 is unethical, because younger children lack the capacity to tell the difference between advertising and information. As the American Academy of Pediatrics reported in 2020, it's generally hard for children under the age of 8 to grasp the point of advertising. That makes them especially susceptible to ads for sugary cereal, toys, video games and fast food. A six-year-old might think that the cartoon character touting a fancy breakfast cereal is just giving them a recommendation for a fun product. They don't realize that the company is paying to say it in order to sell more.

The unethics of advertising to children gets worse when we consider personal data and the digital realm. In 2019, Google reached a $170 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission and New York's Attorney General over the alleged practice of collecting children's personal data on YouTube without appropriate parental consent. But even when there's no data collection, the marketing can blur with the play in online games. Kids might not even recognize that an in-game prize, influencer video, or unboxing are all part of trying to get them to buy something.

That's not to say that we should just ban all ads that target kids. Advertising can be a way of showing them books to read, educational programs, sports gear or healthy food. And of course businesses need advertising to employ people and foster competition. But there need to be ethical boundaries because kids are less experienced, less financially independent, and less critical thinkers than adults. Businesses shouldn't exploit children with manipulation, disguised sponsorship, deceptive health claims, or coercion of their parents. And they shouldn't try to collect their data for customized ads.

Parents have a role to play, but it's not fair to leave it all to them to deal with when companies are using armies of psychologists, designers, data analysts to work on kids. A reasonable approach would be to ban targeted ads for kids under 12. Make it clear when things are sponsored. Put limits on unhealthy food ads during kids' programming. And enforce strong punishments for violations. All to give kids choices, but to protect their new independence. Ethical advertising has to treat childhood as a time of learning and development, not just as an opportunity to be profitable customers.

In the last part of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), Huck has a crucial choice to make as to his moral development. Should he write to Miss Watson, and let her know where her runaway slave, Jim, is? Or should he "go to hell" and destroy the letter?

Huck's initial, sinful impulse is to write the note to Jim's owner (in Hannibal-based St. Petersburg). He feels "washed clean of sin" for a second or two, and then he thinks of the thousand miles they've floated down the Mississippi, and the fog at Cairo, and Jim calling him "honey," and taking care of him like a father. And with the letter in his hand, Huck trembles, and remembers the quick prayer he said, and then says "All right, then, I'll go to hell!" and rips it up into two pieces.

It's a crucial scene because it's Huck's conscience being shattered by his society, not his own evil. He's been brought up by Sunday school, and Widow Douglas, that stealing and condemning a slave is a bad thing. Doing the "right thing" is a betrayal of your friend, in Huck's world. Twain's irony is acute: it's when Huck does his most moral act that he perceives himself to be a sinner. And Huck, by opting for eternal torment instead of Jim's re-enslavement, is throwing out not only Miss Watson's claims to property, but her entire set of values. So Huck grows as a person, in his decision to rely on his own "sound heart" -- as it comes out of his own life experience -- instead of his culture's "deformed conscience." (Twain used these terms in his notebook in 1895 to discuss the central issue in the novel.)

What Huck does is also a victory of the empathetic over abstract ethical statements. Huck can't think his way to abolitionism -- he doesn't have a political philosophy. What he has are memories -- of Jim's grief over his daughter, 'Lizabeth, the one he slapped and didn't know she was deaf; of Jim's delight when he saw that Huck survived the feud with the Grangerfords; of their arguments about King Solomon and the Frenchmen, out there on the raft, like family... Huck's ethics consist of a series of moments when he sees shared humanity.

Critics are right to point out that the novel's conclusion, where Tom Sawyer makes a game out of Jim's already-granted freedom, throws a negative light on Huck's development -- but not so negative that it's cancelled out. And by Huck's "going to hell," Twain argues that conscience isn't something out there, set in a compass handed down by society; conscience is something you build, made up of individual choices -- loyalty, love, etc. Huck doesn't become a respectable person. He becomes a good person.

At the conclusion of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), Huck has a moral test to determine his moral character: Should he write to Miss Watson telling her where her runaway slave, Jim, is? Or should he "go to hell" and destroy the letter? Huck feels "washed clean of sin" when he scrawls the letter to Jim's master in St. Petersburg (of Hannibal fame). But then he remembers that they've floated down the Mississippi a thousand miles; he remembers fog in Cairo; he remembers Jim calling him "honey" and treating him as a father. As he clutches his letter, Huck shakes; he thinks of his brief prayer. Finally he declares, "All right, then, I'll go to hell." Huck tears the letter into pieces.

Why does this act matter so much? Huck's conscience has been broken by society, not by his own evil nature. He has learned in Sunday School and from Widow Douglas that aiding a slave escape is stealing and damned. In this world, if Huck wants to do the "right thing," he must betray his friend. Twain's irony is cutting. Huck believes he's a sinner at the moment he's most moral. And by opting for eternal damnation rather than Jim's reenslavement, Huck refuses the property rights of Miss Watson. Huck also refuses a set of values. Huck's moral development is about coming to rely on his own experience (his "sound heart") rather than the "deformed conscience" of his culture. Twain used this latter expression in his notebook of 1895 to sum up the issue at the center of the novel.

Huck's act also shows the triumph of empathy over a set of abstract principles. Huck can't talk himself into abolitionism. He has no political philosophy. He has his memories of Jim's grief for his daughter, 'Lizabeth, whom Jim slapped before discovering she was deaf. Jim's exuberance at Huck's survival in the feud with the Grangerfords. Huck and Jim bickering over King Solomon and Frenchmen on the raft as if they were a family. Huck's ethics come from a series of moments of common humanity. Not from doctrine.

True enough, the conclusion of the novel—with Tom Sawyer complicating Jim's already-achieved freedom—undermines Huck's development. But not in a way that cancels it out. In "going to hell," Twain makes clear that conscience isn't some ready-made magnetic compass given by society. Conscience is something a person constructs from their own acts, their own loyalties, their own love. Huck doesn't become a respectable person. He becomes a good person.

From 1849 until 1860 or so, Harriet Tubman returned to slave-holding territory in the south roughly 13 times.  These trips were a willful breach of federal law.  The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 not only prohibited the slaves themselves from escaping from slavery, it criminalized assisting others to escape, with the punishment of up to a $1000 fine and imprisonment.  It denied accused runaway slaves a trial by jury.  It required all free citizens in the North to forcibly aid in the capture of runaways, if called upon.  Harriet Tubman, herself a runaway from slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland in 1849, replied to the Fugitive Slave Act by returning into the area specifically targeted by the Act. 

Tubman subverted the Fugitive Slave Act by operating counter to its purpose.  She moved by night, often in the winter months when there would be fewer patrols and the night would be longer.  She used the North Star and the oral networks that became known as the Underground Railroad to guide people to the north.  And after 1850, when the reach of the Fugitive Slave Act into the free states made Philadelphia and even New York no longer a safe destination, Tubman expanded the route north to St. Catharines, Ontario in Canada, where escapees could find protection under the laws of Great Britain and be beyond the jurisdiction of US Marshals.  Tubman guided approximately 70 enslaved people to freedom personally.  Among the people she guided to freedom were members of her own family.  She did this under a rumored $40,000 bounty for her capture.

What distinguishes Tubman's missions from just being a runaway is that they were repeated.  The Act relied on the fear of punishment as a deterrent to keep the line closed one way.  Tubman returned to the other side of the line - the most dangerous direction - repeatedly to extract others.  In addition to using a pistol for her own protection, she reportedly used her pistol to force along those that got weak and tried to go back and compromise the group.  She expanded her acts of defiance against the Act during the Civil War when she served as a scout and spy for the Union Army and assisted in the leading the Combahee River raid of 1863 in South Carolina, which liberated over 700 slaves in one night.

The 13 missions of Harriet Tubman demonstrate that the Fugitive Slave Act, as harsh as it was, was no match for someone who would regard the penalties of the Act as the price one had to pay to do the job, not as a deterrent from doing the job.

During the time period of 1849-1860 Harriet Tubman is credited with completing approximately 13 trips back into the slave-holding South. Each trip was a direct challenge to the federal law. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made not only escaping from slavery a crime. But also assisting anyone else who attempted to do so. The act set a fine of up to $1,000 and potential jail time for anyone considered an abettor. It also deprived alleged fugitives of a jury trial. It forced all free citizens in the North to participate in any capture at will. Tubman had escaped from slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland back in 1849. She had a response to this Act. She challenged it by returning directly into the area it was supposed to cover. 
 Tubman did this in a way that subverted the entire process in the Act. She would do her trips at night, often during winter months. There was less patrolling and the night would be longer. Tubman used the North Star along with oral references to other people. This became known as the Underground Railroad. She would help guide people to the North. She would expand her route after 1850. The reach of the Act in free states made the end destinations in Philadelphia and even New York too risky. Tubman expanded to St. Catharines, Ontario in Canada. Escapees in Canada were protected by British law. They were out of reach of U.S. marshals. 
 Tubman is credited with leading about 70 slaves to freedom herself. This includes family members. Tubman did this all while the bounty for her capture was allegedly rumored to be $40,000. 
 What made these missions a direct challenge to the Act, as opposed to a mere escape, was that she kept coming back. The Act was based on the assumption that fear would be the lock on the border in only one direction. Tubman would cross the border time and time again. Quick answer, yes, it's completely normal to be sore at 6wks post acl reconstruction, however the 'type' of soreness you experience is important. 
 I'm 4m post ham tendon acl (op done at Johns Hopkins on 2/14) and at 6 weeks I still was experiencing daily aching, primarily around the surgical incision sites as well as down the inside of the knee (where they took the hamstring tendon). My PT said it's normal as at 6 weeks you're in the weakest healing phase of the graft (ligamentization stage) and you're probably starting to do more (walk more, stationary bike, leg press potentially, etc) which means you're stressing the tissue in new ways. 
 So at 6 weeks you'll notice: 
 Normal:
 - Ache after pt, or after being on your feet a lot.
 - Tenderness around the portal incisions and donor site
 - Tightness after sitting for extended periods
 - Mild swelling that resolves after laying down overnight. 
 Abnormal that you should call your surgeon for: 
 - Sudden/sharp pain (especially with a pivot)
 - Significant swelling that doesn't resolve with ice/elevating.
 - Warmth, redness, fever (possible infection. Don't fuck around if this is happening.)
 - Unstable knee, feeling of "giving out"
 - Pain in calf (could be clot)
 
 The way my surgeon put it is pain should be improving week-on-week, albeit with potential fluctuations day to day. If you're soreness is plateauing or worsening over 2 weeks you should check in. 
 For me I did lots of icing 15-20 minutes after PT. I also tried to do quads and heel slides on days where I was sore (motion helps) and sleep with a pillow under my knee. Also make sure you're not limping. Limping (hip compensating) results in hip soreness which can get confused with knee soreness. 
 That said, I'm an internet dude not your surgeon. If you feel something's off, call your surgeon's office. Most surgeons have a nurse line and they'd rather you ask a 'stupid' question than fail to note a potential complication. 6 weeks is early in the game. Most people aren't 'good' until 3-4 months.

TLDR: Yes, it's perfectly normal to still be sore at 6 weeks post ACL reconstruction. But it depends on the KIND of soreness 
 4 months after my hamstring graft ACL reconstruction (at Hopkins, surgery date 2/14). At 6 weeks, I was still having daily achiness. Especially at incision sites and on the inside of the knee, where they took the hamstring tendon. My PT was saying it's normal, because at 6 weeks your graft is in its most "weak" healing stage (ligamentization) and you're probably increasing activity (more walking, stationary bike, possibly leg presses now), putting it under different stresses. 
 
 Normal at 6 weeks:
 Dull aches after PT sessions / long walks, etc.
 Soreness around the portal incisions and where they took the tissue
 Stiff if you sit for a while in the same position
 Some mild swelling which goes down overnight 
 
 NOT normal and you should call your surgeon about it:
 Sudden sharp pain, especially if it's like a twist
 Noticeable new swelling, which doesn't seem to go down with icing and elevation
 Warmth, redness, or fever (possibly an infection.  Definitely don't put this off!)
 Feeling unstable in the knee, or that your knee "gives out"
 Calf pain (could be a blood clot) 
 
 General rule of thumb from my surgeon is that, ideally, the pain should be improving gradually week to week (although day to day it may fluctuate).  If you're not seeing any improvement (or getting worse) over a 2 week period, you should have it checked. 
 Some things that helped me were: ice (15-20 minutes) after PT sessions. Try to do quad sets, heel slides on sore days (movement is good). Sleep with a pillow under your knee.  Make sure you're not limping.  Any favoring with the hip will create its own pain and you'll confuse that as knee pain. 
 
 But again, I'm just a random dude on the internet and not your surgeon.  If you have concerns, call their office.  Most surgeons will have a nurse you can call, and they'd much rather you call with a "dumb" question to make sure they don't miss any complications.  At 6 weeks you're still pretty early.  Most people don't feel "good" until 3-4 months.

Oven is better, (or toaster oven/air fryer). Microwave makes the crust rubbery cardboard because it's just heating the moisture in the breading. 
 The real answers. 
 - bring chicken to room temperature (20-30 min) before reheating so it cooks more evenly (you will have a hard time getting it hot in the middle from cold->hot if you reheat from fridge). 
 - heat oven to 400F/200C. Put a wire rack in a sheet pan (this is important, most people skip it). This lets air circulate underneath to prevent it from steaming and getting soggy (which will happen if you just put it on the sheet). 
 - Cook bone in for 15-20 minutes or boneless/tenders for 10-12 minutes. Flip it halfway through. 
 You're looking for the internal temperature to be 165F/74C. You can use a instant read thermometer in the thickest part, close to bone. 
 - do not cover in foil or anything. This traps steam which is bad. 
 *you can also use air fryer which is even faster and may get it crunchier. 375F/190C for 4-6 min. No flipping because it's circulating the air.
I've used it to reheat leftover KFC thighs (like chicken) and Popeye's tenders, it comes pretty close to the fresh crispyness.* 
 Another trick, if the crust still feels a bit soft after reheating, is you can put it under the broiler for the last 60-90sec. Just pay attention it doesn't burn! This direct heat will help crisp the areas that convection oven didn't get to. 
 You don't want to do the microwave unless you don't care about the crust. It will make the crust noticeably softer even if you do it for 30 sec.

Your best bet is to use an oven (better yet, toaster oven / air fryer) rather than a microwave. Microwave turns crust into rubbery cardboard as it heats the trapped moisture in the breading. 
 Instead: 
 1. Bring chicken to room temp for 20-30 minutes before reheating. Reheating cold-to-hot (from fridge) tends to lead to uneven cooking and you end up overcooking the outside of the meat to get the middle warm. 
 2. Preheat oven to 400°F (200°C).
 Put wire rack on sheet pan.
 This is an important step that people often forget.
 Circulation of air below will prevent the bottoms from steaming/getting soggy like it will if you put them directly on sheet pan. 
 3. Cook bone-in for 15-20 minutes.
 Bone-less/tenders for 10-12 minutes.
 Flip them over once.
 You want internal temp to be 165°F (74°C).
 Use instant read meat thermometer to check for this in thickest part of meat near bone. 
 4. Don't cover with foil or anything.
 Covering will trap steam and defeat the purpose. 
 If you happen to have an air fryer then it will be even faster and maybe even crisper.
 You would cook them at 375°F (190°C) for 4-6 minutes.
 You don't need to flip them because there is air circulation all around.
 I did this with leftovers KFC-style thigh meat.
 Also did this with leftovers Popeye's tenders.
 They were both almost as crispy as if they were fresh. 
 If the crust still seems somewhat soft after reheating then for the final 60-90 seconds you can try putting them under broiler.
 Watch carefully so they don't burn.
 This direct heat blast at the end will further crisp up any areas that might have been missed by the convection. 
 Don't even bother with microwave unless you just don't care about crust.
 Even 30 seconds of microwave will make them noticeably less crisp.
