Clean toothpick and dense banana bread is an obvious sign of both underbaking and too much moisture. Also, don't trust the toothpick. Bananas add a ton of water to the batter which will make the middle very gummy and dense even if the starches have solidified to the point of a skewer not sticking. 
 1. Your oven is probably at the wrong temp. Buy an oven thermometer ($8 at target). My GE oven was 25F low. The outside would cook and solidify way before the middle. I find that most dense middles are due to this. 
 2. Use temp instead of toothpick. 200-205 F for banana bread in the middle is when it's done. I use a thermapen. Anything that does instant read is fine. Take it out at 200F and it'll get done perfectly with carryover cooking. 
 3. You probably have too much banana. Most recipes call for 1c smashed (3 medium or ~240g). If you're using 5 large bananas "cuz they're going bad" that's probably an extra .5cup of liquid. You're not going to cook that banana out, it's just going to be gummy. Freeze them. 
 4. Leavening. Baking soda doesn't last forever. If you've been using a can since 2023 then it's time to replace it. Put some in hot water to test. If it doesn't go crazy it's bad. 
 5. Cook at lower temp and longer. Try 325F instead of 350F and cook 60-75 min in a 9x5 pan. Slower cooking helps the middle keep up with the outside. Cover with foil at 45 if it's browning too fast. 
 6. Don't overmix. Just mix until the flour is gone. It will be more chewy and dense if you're developing gluten. 
 7. Allow to cool completely in pan (at least an hour). If you slice it warm the middle will seem dense and more wet than it is. 
 
 If I had to pick, buy a thermometer and cook to 200-205F. That was the only thing I changed to fix this (and I was dealing with dense bread for 2 years!)

Your banana bread is probably both underbaked AND overmoist.  This manifests as dense, clean toothpick.  But the toothpick test is a red herring here.  Bananas add so much moisture to your batter.  Even when your starches set up enough that they don't stick to the skewer, it can be gummy and dense in the middle.  Here's what I'd try: 
 1. Your oven temperature is probably off.  Invest in an oven thermometer (~$8 at Target)  Old GE oven was 25F off for me.  Leading to exterior setting up way earlier than interior.  Almost always the culprit of dense interior. 
 2. Internal temperature is better indicator.  Banana bread done in the middle is ~200-205F.  I use a Thermapen.  Any instant read thermometer.  If you pull it off at 200F it will finish its carryover cooking nicely. 
 3. You're probably using too much banana.  Most recipes call for around 1 cup of mashed (so like 3 medium sized, or ~240g)  if you're using 5 large ones (cause they're going bad) you've probably added like half a cup of extra liquid.  Excess banana doesn't bake away.  It'll be gummy.  If you have extras, freeze it. 
 4.  Check your leavening.  Baking soda can lose potency quickly.  If your baking soda has been open since 2023, swap it out.  Try it in hot water.  If it doesn't vigorously fizz, discard. 
 5.  Lower temp, longer time.  Try 325F instead of 350F.  For 60-75min.  9x5 pan.  This will give the interior more time to catch up to the edges with the slower baking.  You can also tent the top with foil after 45min if it's browning too quickly. 
 6.  Don't over mix.  Just mix until the flour is incorporated.  Gluten development will lead to it being chewy and dense. 
 7.  Let it cool in the pan completely.  (At least an hour)  If you slice a warm banana bread, it will appear dense and more moist in the middle. 
 
The thing that I'd most likely guess is your culprit would be get the thermometer and cook it to 200-205F.  That was the single adjustment that fixed this problem for me after two years of dense banana bread.

Because in JavaScript we store all numbers as IEEE 754 double precision floating points and 0.1, 0.2 can't be represented exactly so it's stored as the closest approximation to that number. In JS 0.1 is actually stored as ~0.1000000000000000055511151231257827 and 0.2 is ~0.200000000000000011102230246251565.

When you add those numbers and round it to the closest double that's representable you end up with 0.30000000000000004, instead of 0.3. But it's not only JS, you get the same result in Python, Java, C and all languages that use standard floating point numbers (IEEE 754) for arithmetic.

Try to type `0.1 + 0.2` in node console or any modern browser console and you will see it right away.

So when it comes to money, don't ever use floats for arithmetic that you're gonna compare/add. 1. Just use int cents/minor units for money. e.g. if you have $19.99 store that as 1999 (int), do all your math with integers and just divide by 100 if you want to display the number. It's the simplest solution and works until you want fractional cents or big money amounts.

2. Use some decimal lib. e.g. decimal.js, big.js, bignumber.js where it represents your numbers as base-10 decimal number. So `0.1 + 0.2` will always result in 0.3 E.g. `new Decimal('0.1').plus('0.2').toString()` will return `"0.3"`.

3. If you don't need decimals in the middle, then use native BigInt for whole cents and just use integers for that (since bigInts won't have float precision issues if we're dealing with big numbers).

4. If it's a modern environment, then be aware of the problems with new Number.prototype.toFixed problems. You should know that .toFixed() won't solve your precision problem, it will just round to a specific string, so don't use it for actual calculations, only for pretty display of the number.

Basically floats for stuff like measurements, graphics. Ints or dec lib for money.

That's because JavaScript uses IEEE 754 double precision floating-point for number storage, and there is no precise binary representation of 0.1 or 0.2. The numbers end up being represented as the closest representable value. 0.1 is "actually" stored as ~0.1000000000000000055511151231257827 and 0.2 as ~0.200000000000000011102230246251565. If you now add them and take the closest representable double number, it comes out to 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. This isn't a Javascript specific problem, it's the same in python, java, c, and any other language that uses standard floating point numbers (IEEE 754). Just open up a node.js console or your browser dev tools and type '0.1 + 0.2' and see for yourself.

If you need to do any kind of math with money that you need to compare / add up, you shouldn't be using plain float arithmetic. Some good approaches are:

1) use integer cents (or some kind of minor unit). Store $19.99 as 1999 (int) do all the math with integer and only divide by 100 for display. This is the most straight forward solution. It works until you want to do fractions or huge sums.

2) Use a decimal package. Things like decimal.js or big.js or bignumber.js have base-10 decimals instead of binary floats. So your 0.1 + 0.2 will in fact be 0.3. Like new Decimal('0.1').plus('0.2').toString() => "0.3"

3) If you don't need to deal with decimals in the middle of the calculation, use native BigInt to do integer (whole cent) math if you don't need floats (so you avoid float precision issues with BigInt on large integers).

4) In newer environment you'll also want to be careful about what's coming with the new Number.prototype.toFixed stuff as well. toFixed() doesn't solve the precision problem. It just rounds for display. So don't use it for actual math. Just use it for the presentation.

For money use integer (or decimal lib) not floats. Use float for things like measurements and graphics.

You are doing this. This is good. 
 For a basic 15 amp circuit with 120V, maximum you can draw is 1800W 
 You have to load a circuit only to 80% max per NEC, so that means you actually only get 1440W as a safe max 
 Typical microwave is 1000-1500W. (Example: if you have a 1,200W microwave, that means you're pulling 1500W from the wall because it's not 100% efficient) 
 Typical toaster 800-1500W. (Like 900-1200W for a typical 2 slice) 
 
 If you use a 1200W microwave and a 1000W toaster at the same time that's about 2200W. Exceeds your 1800W max. Your breaker is doing it's job. Protecting your wire from getting too hot. 
 
 To fix this: 
 1) Just don't use it at the same time. Make the toast first, then microwave. Sucks but it's free 
 2) Try to plug one into a different circuit. If your kitchen was built after mid 90's, it's code to have at least 2 20a small appliance circuits at countertop. If you have only 1 15a circuit that supplies everything in your kitchen, that's a big flag that your kitchen isn't up to modern code. You can plug the toaster into an outlet on a different wall. It might be on a separate breaker. If you plug a light (lamp) into each one, and switch breakers off, you can figure out where all the outlets are wired to. 
 3) Upgrade! If your kitchen is only supplied by 1 15a circuit, usually you're looking at $300-600 to have an electrician add in a 20a small appliance circuit. It's worth it if you cook a lot. 
 
 Do NOT replace 15a breaker with 20a breaker. Breaker size is designed to protect wire gauge. 15a breaker will protect 14 gauge wire. If you put a bigger breaker on it, it can overheat in your walls and never trip. Fires happen this way. 
 
 TL:DR Your microwave and toaster together use too much. Breaker isn't broken. It's saving your house.

This is actually normal and here's why. 
 120V, 15A standard circuit can supply up to 1800W.  However, according to National Electrical Code, you're not supposed to run at more than 80% of that continuously. So you've got about 1440W to play with safely. 
 Let's go over your appliances: 
 Microwave is usually 1000-1500W (a 1200W microwave will draw about 1500W from the wall. It's not 100% efficient) 
 Toaster is 800-1500W (A common 2 slice is about 900-1200W) 
 So, using a 1200W microwave and 1000W toaster you're going to be drawing about 2200W. That's definitely more than your 1800W limit. So, your breaker is tripping because it's doing its job and preventing overheating of your wiring. 
 
 So, you can: 
 Don't use them at the same time. Toast, then microwave. It's a pain, but free. 
 Plug one into a different circuit. Modern kitchens (since mid 90's) usually have to be coded with 2 20A small appliance circuits at the countertop. If you have only 1 15A that runs everything in your kitchen that's a sign that you probably have wiring from before modern codes. Try plugging in the toaster in an outlet on a different wall. Maybe it's on a different breaker. You can test by plugging a lamp into each and trying to figure out which breakers cut which outlets. One at a time. 
 Upgrade. If you've only got 1 15A circuit in your kitchen, then getting an electrician to install 20A small appliance circuit typically costs $300-600 and worth it if you do a lot of cooking. 
 
 Do NOT just swap the 15A breaker for 20A. Breaker sizes are based on the size of the wire they are protecting. 15A breakers protect 14gauge wire. You may end up causing overheating of wire in your walls without even tripping the breaker if you install a larger breaker. That's how you get electrical fires. 
 
 TL;DR 
 Microwave and toaster draw more than what the circuit can provide. It's not a faulty breaker. It's saving your house.

Yes. It's perfectly safe and in fact it's a well-researched strategy for treating migraines. Ibuprofen and acetaminophen work in different ways (ibuprofen is a NSAID to reduce inflammation, acetaminophen is a bit more contentious in its mechanism but it works centrally more than anything else) so they're not targeting the same process and can be used together. 
 For an average adult with no other complications, a common way to approach this is taking 400mg ibuprofen with 500mg-1000mg acetaminophen at the start of the migraine. 
 Some OTC combination pills (e.g. Excedrin migraine which is 250mg acetaminophen and 250mg aspirin + 65mg caffeine) follow this "combine different mechanisms" approach. That particular combination uses aspirin instead of ibuprofen. 
 
 Things to keep in mind: 
 Max acetaminophen dose per day is 3000-4000mg for an average healthy adult (more and more clinicians now suggest 3000mg/day max if you use it on a daily basis). So a 500mg dose is definitely in range, even if you repeat the dose 6-8h later. 
 Max OTC ibuprofen dose per day is typically 1200mg/day (400mg every 6h) but if your doctor prescribes it, sometimes the limit can be up to 3200mg/day. 
 Beware of a third product without checking the label! Many so called "migraine" or "sinus" combo pills will include acetaminophen. It's easy to double up and go over the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen that way. 
 
 Be careful if you have liver disease/are a heavy drinker (acetaminophen), and kidney disease/stomach ulcers/GERD or are on blood thinners like warfarin (ibuprofen). If you're pregnant, 65+ or take other regular medication, check with a pharmacist. Takes a couple of minutes at the counter. They'll help you spot possible interactions with your other prescriptions. 
 
 If you have frequent migraines and you're using this combo more than 2-3 times a week, you may want to speak to your doctor about preventative treatment rather than using OTC combos long-term (frequent use can trigger a headache problem called medication overuse headache)

MEMORANDUM

To: Maria Kowalski (CEO) & Jan Freitag (CTO)
From: Elena Rasmussen (DPO)
Date: 12 May 2025
Re: GDPR Retention Compliance: Kowalski Customer Database EU Expansion

Purpose. This memo reviews our GDPR data retention requirements and steps needed in advance of 1 September 2025 EU expansion (new markets Germany, Netherlands & Poland) for our Kowalski customer database.

Key Requirements
(1) Specific retention periods. (Article 5(1)(e): "not be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed." Our practice of indefinitely storing inactive customer data is non-compliant. Proposal: transactional data (7 years, per Poland & Germany tax laws); marketing preference/consent (as long as consent valid + 3 years for audit trail); abandoned cart browse data (max 90 days).
(2) Automated data deletion. By 15 Aug 2025 Engineering (P. Nowak team) needs to put automated deletion/anonymization processes in place in our CRM. Manual quarterly data purges won't scale for projected 2.4M new EU customer records.
(3) Minimize data during migration. Can only migrate data fields relevant to order processing/legal compliance. Legacy fields (eg scanned ID docs from 2016-2019 fraud checks) must be deleted prior to migration (not afterward).
(4) Maintain "records of processing" (Art. 30). Need to incorporate retention schedule into our processing inventory (will be scrutinized by our supervisory authority likely Polish UODO, since Warsaw will be primary EU entity for our processing).
(5) Data subject rights. Need to include retention schedules in privacy notices & respond to access/erase requests. Need to account for specific legal holds (eg ongoing Bergmann logistics litigation).

Risk. Non-compliant data retention could result in up to €20M or 4% global turnover fines & weaken our lawful basis for marketing (Art 6(1)(a).

Action & Owners.

1. Approve retention schedule Exec Committee 30 May 2025
2. Delete legacy ID scans IT Ops (L. Hansen) 20 June 2025
3. Automated deletion workflows Engineering (P. Nowak) 15 Aug 2025
4. Update privacy notices/Art. 30 DPO office 22 Aug 2025

Request 30 min at 28 May leadership meeting to finalize retention schedule. Budget impact: €85k for tooling/external counsel review (already included as FY2025 compliance budget line item).

To: Executive Leadership Team
From: Finance & Strategy
Date: September 21, 2026
Re: Q2 FY26 Financial Performance Summary

The Q2 FY26 consolidated revenue was $412.6 MM, +7.1% YoY (Q2 FY25 revenue was $385.2MM). This is driven primarily by strong performance in Medical Devices (+11.4%) and Consumer Diagnostics (+9.2%). Unfortunately, Pharmaceutical division's gross margin declined to 38.4%, vs. Q2 FY25's 44.9% - 650bps reduction. This is the main drag on otherwise positive topline growth that pushes the consolidated operating margin down to 19.8% from 22.3%.

The 3 factors that led to the margin pressure in Pharma are:

1) Cost of active pharmaceutical ingredients from our Hyderabad and Cork sites increased by 14% due to supply disruptions in March/April.

2) Generic substitution ahead of forecast following expiration of Nexovant patent exclusivity (2nd highest revenue branded product) in January, resulted in average selling price reduction of ~18% (U.S. market).

3) Write-downs of $6.2 MM of inventory from discontinued lots in the Raleigh manufacturing site in May.

Since Pharma's revenue was virtually flat (+$148.3M, +0.6% YoY), it is disproportionally adding cost to the overall P&L without contributing revenue growth to offset. It seems likely that we will end up with ~39% gross margin for the full year of Pharma if the trends continue. This is ~500bps less than FY25's 44.1%.

Recommended actions for Q3: 1) Accelerate API dual-sourcing (Basel supplier) to mitigate input cost volatility - by year end.

2) Expedite Nexovant-XR reformulation, target FDA submission date of November 15 to re-establish (partial) branded pricing power.

3) Complete process audit at the Raleigh site by October 10 to avoid any re-occurrence of write-downs.

We will be presenting a comprehensive pharma margin recovery plan to the Board at October 14 meeting.

INTERNAL MEMORANDUM To: Executive Leadership Team and Board Audit & Risk Committee From: Dana Whitfield, Chief Compliance Officer Date: June 14, 2025 Re: Q2 2025 Anti-Money Laundering Training Compliance Status and Remediation

Summary
As of June 10, 2025, we've reached 94% (1,872/1,991) employee completion rate for required annual Anti-Money Laundering training. This is above our internal goal of 90% completion; however, we have 119 employees yet to complete the training. We are in the process of implementing our remediation plan to achieve 100% compliance by July 31, 2025.

 Corporate & Shared Services - 98% (6 Outstanding)

 Retail Banking Operations - 96% (41 Outstanding)

 Commercial Lending - 93% (22 Outstanding)

 Wealth Management - 89% (38 Outstanding)

 International (Singapore, London) - 91% (12 Outstanding)

Note that 100% of 63 licensed relationship managers in Wealth Management have completed the enhanced KYC training module. There are issues with the support staff.

Findings
The largest contributors to non-completion are (1) employees on extended medical/parental leave (27 employees) and (2) employees hired in Q2 yet to be onboarded (44 employees). There are only 48 employees with no explainable reason for non-completion. For the Singapore office, there was a scheduling conflict with the system migration in May; made up sessions were conducted June 3-5.

Remediation Plan
1. June 16-20 - written notices provided by the direct supervisor for the 48 non-completed employees without explainable reason. Employees will be enrolled in required live training sessions on June 24 and July 8. 2. June 30 - for employees returning from leave, we have auto-enrolled employees in training within five business days after their return (HR will confirm via payroll reactivation flags). 3. July 15 - Q2 new hires will be required to complete onboarding training. This is now a requirement for their probationary review. 4. July 31 - we will escalate any remaining non-completers to division heads and limit access to customer facing systems (as per Section 4.3 of the AML Policy). 5. August 5 - provide final attestation report to Board Audit & Risk Committee

Regulatory Requirements
Our regulator mandates that annual refresh training be provided for all employees on Anti-Money Laundering. Our prior year exam reported that 91% completion was satisfactory. However, it recommended that we have a procedure to escalate non-completers. We have incorporated those procedures into the plan.

Budget Considerations
We estimate $18,500 cost for remediation (live session facilitation, LMS licensing). This is within existing budget for FY2025 compliance training of $420,000.

There is no further action to request from our leadership at this time. Our next update will be on August 5.

paper_section_00_glm.text:
Abstract
The hepatic uptake transporter OATP1B1 (encoded by SLCO1B1) is responsible for the uptake of many endogenous compounds and clinically relevant drugs, such as statins, into hepatocytes. OATP1B1 loss-of-function polymorphisms (e.g., rs4149056 T>C polymorphism, c.521T>C; Val174Ala) are common and correlate with increased systemic exposure to statins and higher risk for myopathy. However, the quantitative role of OATP1B1 for the overall hepatocellular uptake of individual substrates is not fully understood. We have developed a CRISPR-Cas9-based OATP1B1 knockout model in HepG2 cells to directly assess the quantitative contribution of the OATP1B1 to hepatocellular uptake. We have used two single guide RNAs that target OATP1B1 exons 2 and 6 to generate clonal OATP1B1 knockout cell lines. Sanger sequencing, RT-qPCR (>95% decrease in transcript level of SLCO1B1), and Western blot (no OATP1B1 protein detected) were used to validate clonal OATP1B1 knockout lines. Whole genome off-target analyses, using targeted amplicon sequencing on top ten predicted off-targets sites, found no indels >1.2% allele frequency. Uptake experiments (37°C, 5 min, 10 µM of fluorescent pravastatin) showed 43.0% ± 3.8% (mean ± SEM, *n* = 4 independent experiments, *p* < 0.001, two-tailed unpaired *t*-test) decrease in uptake in the OATP1B1 knockout clones compared with wild-type HepG2 cells and the non-targeting guide RNA control cells. The remaining uptake was not sensitive to the OATP inhibitor rifampicin (100 µM), but partially sensitive to probenecid. This suggested that other organic anion transporters, probably including OATP1B3 and Na+ -taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide that are still expressed in the OATP1B1 knockout clones, mediate the residual uptake. Kinetic analysis revealed that this reduced uptake is attributed to 46% decrease in the maximal transport capacity (Vmax: 285 ± 31 vs. 528 ± 44 pmol/mg protein/5 min) but with no significant change in apparent Km. Our study provides a direct quantitative assessment of the role of OATP1B1 for the statin uptake in a human hepatocyte model. We have also developed a validated isogenic knockout model that can be used to screen drug disposition in a substrate- and genotype-dependent manner, which has implications for precision dosing of OATP1B1 substrates in carriers of loss-of-function alleles.

Abstract
SLCO1B1-encoded hepatic uptake transporter OATP1B1 facilitates hepatic uptake of many endogenous substrates and clinically relevant drugs (e.g., statins). Loss-of-function alleles in SLCO1B1 (e.g., the prevalent rs4149056 T>C polymorphism (c.521T>C, Val174Ala) that increases circulating statin levels and myopathy risk) can increase systemic statin exposure, but the quantitative role of OATP1B1 in total hepatic uptake of specific substrates is not well understood. In the current study, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to knockout SLCO1B1 in HepG2 cells to directly quantify the contribution of OATP1B1 to hepatic uptake. Using 2 single guide RNAs targeting exon 2 and 6 of SLCO1B1, we identified clonal knockouts of SLCO1B1 confirmed by Sanger sequencing, >95% reduction of SLCO1B1 transcripts as determined by RT-qPCR, and no detectable OATP1B1 protein by Western blot. Whole-genome off-target analysis of top ten predicted off-target sites by targeted amplicon sequencing found no indels with >1.2% allele frequency. Measuring fluorescently-labeled pravastatin (10 µM) uptake at 37ºC for 5 min, we observed a 43.0% ± 3.8% (mean ± SEM, n= 4 independent experiments, p<0.001 (two-tailed unpaired t-test)) decrease in uptake by knockout clones compared to wild type HepG2 cells and non-targeting guide RNA controls. The remaining uptake was not blocked by OATP inhibitor rifampicin (100 µM) but partially by probenecid, indicating it may be mediated by other organic anion transporters (e.g., likely OATP1B3 and Na+-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide still expressed in knockout clones). Uptake decrease was due to a 46% reduction in maximal transport capacity (Vmax: 285±31 vs 528±44 pmol/mg protein/5min) with no significant change in apparent Km from kinetic analysis. This study provides a direct and quantitative measure of OATP1B1's role in statin uptake in a human hepatocyte model, and validates a knockout of OATP1B1 isogenic platform for screening substrate- and genotype-dependent drug disposition and has implications for precision dosing for OATP1B1 substrates in subjects with loss-of-function alleles.

Methods
Participants included 240 veterans (mean age, 47.3 years [SD = 12.1]; 68% male) between March 2021 and November 2022 from outpatient clinics at the VA Puget Sound Health Care System (Seattle, WA) and the VA Boston Healthcare System (Boston, MA). Veterans had DSM-5 chronic insomnia disorder, Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) score ≥15, and no current suicidal ideation or untreated psychosis. Veterans with comorbid PTSD (n = 142; 59%) were included to mimic the population of interest. A total of 412 referrals were screened and 240 were randomized 1:1 into cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I; n = 120) or active control (sleep hygiene education + attention matched contact; n = 120) using a computer-generated permuted block schedule (block size = 4, stratified by site and PTSD).

The CBT-I intervention consisted of 6 weekly 50-minute individual sessions led by 14 doctoral level psychologists (trained to ≥90% criterion on a fidelity standardized checklist), which included sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, and relapse prevention. Participants in the control condition had one 30-minute sleep hygiene session followed by 5 weekly 20-minute check-in calls. Data were collected at baseline, post-treatment (week 7), and 6-month follow-up (May 2023). Primary outcome was ISI score. Secondary outcomes included sleep efficiency (sleep diary), 7 consecutive nights actigraphy (Actiwatch-2), PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) score, and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) score. Outcome assessors were blinded to condition. The sample size was powered at 0.90 to identify a between-group difference of 4 points on the ISI (SD = 6.5) with 15% attrition (α = .05, 2-tailed) (n = 120/arm). The main analyses included intention-to-treat using linear mixed models (random intercept by participant and site) adjusted for baseline ISI and PTSD status. This study was approved by VA Central Institutional Review Board (IRB #2020-0847). It was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04739228). Participants provided written informed consent before randomization.

Methods
Two hundred forty veterans (M age = 47.3 years, SD = 12.1, 68% male) were enrolled from March 2021 to November 2022 from VA Puget Sound Health Care System (Seattle, WA) and VA Boston Healthcare System (Boston, MA) outpatient clinics. Inclusion criteria included DSM-5 chronic insomnia disorder, Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) score ≥15, and no current suicidal ideation or psychosis. Veterans with comorbid PTSD (n = 142, 59%) were included to match the target population. Of 412 referrals, 240 participants were randomized (1:1) to either cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I; n = 120) or active control sleep hygiene education with attention-matched contact (n = 120) via a computer-generated permuted block randomizer (block size 4; stratified by site and PTSD status). CBT-I included 6 weekly 50-min individual therapy sessions administered by 14 doctoral level psychologists with ≥90% fidelity based on a standardized checklist (sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, and relapse prevention). Control group received one 30-min sleep hygiene education session, plus 5 weekly 20-min check in phone calls. Baseline, post-treatment (week 7), and 6-month follow-up assessment (May 2023). Primary outcome was ISI score, secondary outcomes included sleep diary derived sleep efficiency, 7 consecutive nights Actiwatch-2 (actigraphy), PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) score, Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) score. Outcome assessors were blind to condition. Target sample size (n = 120/group) had 0.90 power to detect 4-point between group difference in ISI (SD = 6.5) (assumed 15% attrition, alpha = .05, two tailed). Linear mixed effects models (intention-to-treat) with random participant and site intercepts, controlling for baseline ISI and PTSD were used as the primary analytic model. Study was approved by VA Central Institutional Review Board (IRB#2020-0847) and registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04739228). All participants provided written informed consent before randomization.

paper_section_04_luna.text:
While the Open Science Collaboration's 2015 study is compelling evidence that many of the effects reported in the literature were not as robust as reported, it is a mistake to view the results as evidence that most of the original studies were fraudulent. The Open Science Collaboration set out to replicate 100 studies published in 2008 in *Psychological Science*, *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* and *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition*. The original studies reported a 97% rate of statistically significant results, whereas the replication studies showed only a 36% rate of statistical significance. Not only did only a small fraction of the replications prove statistically significant, but the average effect size of the replications was about half as large as the original effect (r = .197 compared to r = .403), which suggests that often times when replications fail, they do not fail because there is nothing going on at all, but because the original effect was substantially overestimated. [Open Science Collaboration, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716)

There are many reasons that the replication results may differ from the original results: publications are biased towards novel and statistically significant results. Methods of analysis are often flexible and samples are sometimes small, so results are often unstable and unlikely to be replicable. Many original studies may rely on particular cultures, samples, experimenter bias or even details about how procedures were run that make exact replication very difficult. That is, a direct replication failure could very well be due to boundary conditions or methodological differences and not fraud or a completely misguided theory. In fact, in the present study 47% of original effect sizes were inside the 95% confidence interval of the replication study and 39% of findings were deemed replicated by the replication teams.

Still, the difference between the original and replication results is proof that relying on statistical significance for the reliability of science is not enough. The large, preregistered collaborative study was a study that forced a focus on power, effect size estimation, transparency and cumulative evidence. Therefore, the biggest value of the study is not an estimation of what the 'true' replication rate in psychology is, but the empirical evidence that there are ways in which we can be systematically tricked into being more confident in published results. If we are serious about improving reproducibility, we must embrace preregistration, larger samples, open data and materials, registered reports, and tolerance for null results.

Open Science Collaboration in 2015 found strong evidence that published psychology results were much weaker than the literature had lead us to believe. However, these findings don't necessarily mean that most original studies were false. 100 studies published in 2008 in *Psychological Science*, *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, and *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition* were attempted for replication. Even though 97% of original studies produced statistically significant results, only 36% of the replications were statistically significant. Additionally, the mean size of effect of replications was about half that of the original effect (r = .197 vs r = .403), meaning that often replications failed because there was a large overestimation of the effect size, not necessarily because there wasn't any underlying effect at all. [Open Science Collaboration, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716)

This could be due to several methodological and institutional factors. For example, there's a bias towards publishing surprising, statistically significant results (selective publication). Flexible analysis and small samples tend to yield unstable estimates that are less likely to be replicated. Original studies could also be sensitive to particular cultural factors, participant samples, experimenter's expectations or methodological details that are hard to perfectly replicate. In other words, a failure to replicate in a direct replication doesn't necessarily mean that there is deliberate dishonesty or completely wrong theory. Instead, it could just mean boundary conditions or methodological differences. 47% of original effect sizes lay within 95% confidence interval of the replication study and 39% of findings were rated by replication teams as having replicated.

In any case, the difference between the results of original studies vs replications shows that statistical significance isn't enough to guarantee the reliability of science. The fact that it was a big collaborative and preregistered study made us focus on power, estimation of effect size, transparency and accumulation of evidence. The most important message of this study isn't just one estimate of psychology "real" rate of replications, but the empirical evidence showing that research practices can systematically bias our confidence in the results of published research. We need to improve our reproducibility by using preregistration, bigger samples, open data/materials, registered reports, and greater willingness to publish null results.

paper_section_06_glm.text:
Introduction
Starting from September 2021, the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) embarked on a sequence of unorthodox monetary policy rate cuts that would prove to be among the most significant monetary policy experiments in modern times. During the span of about 4 months, the monetary policy rate was lowered from 19% to 14% against a backdrop of annual consumer price inflation approaching 20%. In 2022 and 2023, the process of monetary policy rate cuts continued, reaching 8.5% by February 2023; while, at the same time, the headline inflation rate surged above 80% in October 2022, the highest level ever recorded in Türkiye's republican history. The policy rationale behind this unorthodox policy path, frequently emphasised by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and reflected in the government's economic program declared in December 2021, was anchored on the idea that high interest rates are inflationary, a reversal of standard monetary theory, which became popular in Turkish parlance as " faiz sebep, enflasyon sonuç" (interest is the cause of inflation, inflation is the effect).

The Turkish case represents a rare natural experiment in which a major globally integrated economy explicitly decided to pursue a policy approach that is the exact opposite of the inflation targeting consensus approach, at a time when the global economic environment (post-covid demand recovery, commodity price shock after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022) was already exerting upward pressure on inflation globally. Separating out the domestic policy effect from these global factors is the main empirical task in this paper.

We make three main contributions to the existing literature. First, by putting together a monthly dataset covering January 2010 until December 2023 that contains CBRT policy actions, Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) price indices, sovereign credit default swap spreads and USD/TRY exchange rate movements, we document the temporal evolution and transmission process of the unorthodox easing policy. Second, through a structural vector autoregression (VAR) model combined with a synthetic control approach (versus a weighted basket of emerging market economy peers including Brazil, South Africa and Poland) we attempt to quantify the counterfactual inflation development in the absence of the rate cuts. Third, we explore the behavioural side of the story, in particular, on the basis of surveys, from TÜİK's consumer expectation surveys as well as CBRT's market participants polls, we document the process of inflation expectations becoming unanchored, which reached 12 month ahead inflation expectations above 60% in the middle of 2022.

The Turkish story, which eventually concluded with an orthodox policy shift under Governor Hafize Gaye Erkan (June 2023), with rate increases from 8.5% to 40% in the course of six months, is of relevance for the ongoing discussion on the consequences of giving up institutional monetary frameworks, pass through of exchange rates in high dollarisation, as well as central bank independence and politics. The Turkish case, with all its twists and turns, represents a rather cautionary natural experiment that is far beyond the boundaries of Türkiye.

Introduction
In September 2021, Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) began a sequence of unconventional policy rate cuts.

It was a decisive move that would become the backdrop for one of the most important monetary policy experiments of modern times. Starting in September 2021, the policy rate was cut from 19% to 14% over a period of around 4 months. Even while the annual inflation rate was close to 20%.

That trend continued through 2022 and 2023. The policy rate was reduced further to as low as 8.5% in February 2023, even though by October 2022 headline inflation reached 80%+ (the highest in Türkiye's republican history). The intellectual basis behind this move (repeatedly emphasised by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and part of the government's economic program published in December 2021) was the idea that high interest rates are inflationary in and of themselves, turning conventional monetary economics on its head.

And, in Turkish vernacular, this principle became known as " faiz sebep, enflasyon sonuç" (interest is the cause, inflation is the result). What we have here is a unique natural experiment.

One where a big open economy made a very conscious decision to completely ignore the conventional wisdom of inflation targeting. It was also an experiment that happened at a time when global factors (post-pandemic demand rebound, the commodity price shock caused by the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022) were already pointing to general inflation rise. The task of untangling what was domestic policy from global factors is the main empirical question we need to tackle in this paper.

We provide three main contributions. First, we build a monthly dataset (January 2010 -December 2023) which includes CBRT policy moves, Turkish Statistics Institute (TÜİK) price indices, credit default swap spreads (for sovereign) and USD/TRY currency movements to show the sequence of events and mechanism behind the unconventional easing policy. Second, we use a structural vector autoregression model (with a synthetic control exercise comparing Türkiye with weighted emerging market group such as Brazil, South Africa, Poland etc.) to quantify what would have been the counterfactual inflation path in the absence of the policy rate cuts. Third, we focus on the behavioural side of the story.

We have survey data from the TÜİK consumer expectation surveys, and also CBRT's market participant surveys. These provide us with the evolution of inflation expectations in the period, showing how they became increasingly de-anchored (12 month ahead expectations were > 60% in the middle of 2022). Our results have implications for the cost of policy departure from institutional frameworks, exchange rate pass-through dynamics in highly dollarised economies, political economy of central bank independence.

The Turkish experience, which culminated in a shift to orthodox policy (under the new governor Hafize Gaye Erkan in June 2023; the policy rate going from 8.5% to 40% in 6 months) is a cautionary natural experiment that is by no means specific to Türkiye.

Results
The effect of laser power (150 W, 175 W, 200 W, 225 W, and 250 W) on the tensile response of Ti-6Al-4V specimens produced using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) on the EOS M290 was studied (with scan speed fixed at 1200 mm/s, hatch distance at 0.10 mm and layer thickness at 30 μm). Ten dog-bone (ASTM E8 sub-size) specimens were printed for each condition. They were stress-relieved at 650 • C for 3 h in Ar and tested in tension (to failure) on Instron 5985 (1 mm/min crosshead speed).

The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) increased from 1021 ± 18 MPa (150 W) to a maximum of 1147 ± 12 MPa (200 W), then decreased to 1089 ± 24 MPa (225 W) and 1043 ± 31 MPa (250 W) (mean ± SD; n = 10). One-way ANOVA showed laser power to have a significant influence on UTS (F(4,45) = 26.7, p < 0.001). Tukey HSD posthoc tests indicated that 200 W differed significantly from all other conditions (p < 0.01; except 225 W, p = 0.08). Similar trends were seen in yield strength (e.g., 1068 ± 15 MPa at 200 W; 948 ± 21 MPa at 150 W). A maximum elongation to fracture was seen for 200 W (11.4 ± 0.9%) while a large drop was observed for 250 W (6.2 ± 1.3%). This was associated with an increase in porosity (0.8 vs. 2.9% by micro-CT respectively), which was linked to the instability of the keyhole-mode process at higher energy densities.

The fractographic examination of 250 W samples (SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300) showed the presence of spherical keyhole pores (30-80 μm diameter) in particular at the fracture origin location -which corresponded to lower ductility observed. In contrast, lack-of-fusion defects (non-spherical morphology) were seen in 150 W samples, which is associated with lower UTS despite similar overall porosity level (1.1%). The data shows that the optimum condition for maximising the strength-ductility trade-off within the studied laser power range (with the studied fixed scan parameters) is 200 W.

Results

The tensile mechanical properties of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) fabricated Ti-6Al-4V specimens were investigated under different laser powers (150, 175, 200, 225 and 250 W) using the EOS M290 machine at a constant scan speed (1200 mm/s), hatch spacing (0.10 mm) and layer thickness (30 μm). 10 dog bone specimens (ASTM E8 subsize) were printed for each condition, stress relieved at 650 • C for 3 h in Ar, then loaded to fracture at 1 mm/min crosshead speed using an Instron 5985 testing machine.

The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) increased from 1021 ± 18 MPa (150 W) to a maximum of 1147 ± 12 MPa (200 W), then dropped to 1089 ± 24 MPa (225 W) and 1043 ± 31 MPa (250 W) (mean ± SD, n = 10). A one-way ANOVA was conducted, and significant differences between groups were found for UTS (F (4,45) = 26.7, p < 0.001). A Tukey HSD test revealed a significant difference between the 200 W group and all other groups (p < 0.01) except 225 W (p = 0.08). A similar trend was observed for yield strength, with a maximum of 1068 ± 15 MPa (200 W) compared to 948 ± 21 MPa (150 W). The maximum elongation to break was at 200 W (11.4 ± 0.9%), while the lowest was at 250 W (6.2 ± 1.3%) accompanied by a higher percentage of porosity (0.8% vs. 2.9% micro-CT) due to the instability of keyhole mode with higher energy density.

250 W fracture surfaces examined by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300) showed spherical (keyhole) pores (30-80 μm diameter) were concentrated around the fracture origin and linked to the low ductility. At 150 W, the lack of fusion (LOF) defects of irregular morphology were found and associated with lower UTS value although they had a similar level of porosity (1.1% overall). The findings suggest that 200 W is the best laser power for the selected set of scan parameters to achieve the best combination of strength and ductility within the range studied.

paper_section_10_luna.text:
Effects of British Columbia’s carbon tax on manufacturing plant GHG emissions: A 2019 policy perspective

British Columbia enacted a revenue neutral carbon tax in 2008. Yet, as of April 2019, the British Columbia provincial carbon tax rate (per tonne of CO 2 equivalent) rose to C$40, sending a strong price signal for the consumption of fossil fuels. We use confidential fuel expenditure data from individual manufacturing plant level data on emissions, output, and employment to build a manufacturing emissions panel data set. We estimate an augmented difference in differences model to assess effects of the carbon tax on greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing plants, using variations across plants in their exposures to the carbon tax. This is done in relative comparisons between more carbon intensive and less exposed plants, accounting for plant and year fixed effects, sectoral trends, and general economic conditions.

Based on our empirical analysis, we find that manufacturing plant GHG emissions decreased by about 4% from the counterfactual trend, mostly due to a decrease in the GHG emissions intensity (about 6%) accompanied by an increase in the plant output (about 1.8%). Thus, the effect is not simply through contraction of manufacturing activities, or plant closures. Rather, firms seemed to have responded by generating more output using less fossil fuel energy, which may imply investment in energy efficiency or productivity enhancement technologies. To the extent that the tax revenue was returned through corporate income tax cuts and other actions (a revenue neutral policy design), the cost of abatement investment may have been reduced.

Thus, British Columbia’s carbon pricing policy is found to have led to noticeable emission reductions in manufacturing, without adversely affecting aggregate output of manufacturing plants. Yet, it is important to note that the estimated effects are not necessarily the standalone effects of a new 2019 tax given that the policy began in 2008, and the 2019 tax rate can be seen as an escalation of the 2008 program.

The effect of the British Columbia carbon tax on emissions from manufacturing plants in 2019.

British Columbia implemented a revenue-neutral carbon tax in 2008. However, the carbon tax rate at the provincial level jumped to C$40 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) in April 2019, offering a strong signal on fossil fuel use. This paper investigates the impact of the BC carbon tax on emissions from manufacturing plants in 2019. We use confidential plant-level data on fuel expenditures, emissions, output, employment, to build a panel for manufacturing emissions and employ an augmented difference-in-difference estimation approach. Our model takes advantage of the variation in plants' exposure to the tax and compares more carbon-intensive plants to less exposed ones. We control for plant and year fixed effects, sectoral patterns, as well as general economic circumstances.

Our results show that manufacturing plant greenhouse gas emissions decreased by about 4% compared to what would have happened otherwise due to the carbon tax. The results suggest that emissions intensity dropped by about 6% while the plant output rose by 1.8% or so. This implies that emissions are not falling because of contraction in manufacturing or plant closures, but rather due to firms producing more output using less fossil-fuel energy, perhaps by deploying energy efficiency technologies and productivity-enhancing technologies. The revenue-neutral nature of the tax that recycles revenues from the carbon tax through corporate income tax cuts and other measures may help with such adjustment by lowering the abatement investment costs.

Our results show that in British Columbia's carbon-pricing scheme there are measurable emissions reductions in manufacturing without the need to reduce the total plant output. However, one needs to note that our estimates do not reflect an effect of a new tax in 2019 but rather reflect an effect of the policy that started in 2008. The rate in 2019 was an escalation of that policy.

Methods

In situ TEM cell configuration
In situ TEM measurements on the open-cell configuration were performed on a FEI Titan 80-300 environmental TEM at 300 kV. The camera was a Gatan OneView with 25 frames/s continuous imaging. The nanoscale electrochemical cell was prepared in a Hummingbird Scientific electrical biasing TEM holder. A half-cell approach is followed where a lithium metal electrode with ~100 nm thick Li 2 O coating is prepared by scratching metallic Li (99.9%, Sigma Aldrich) foil using a tungsten wire and using native Li 2 O as a solid electrolyte layer. As the counter electrode, a sharp, electrochemically polished Cu wire (99.99%, Alfa Aesar, 250 μm diameter) is used. The Cu wire is contacted to the surface of Li 2 O using piezoerically actuated, sub-10 nm positioning resolution manipulation.

Electrochemical measurements
The Keithley 2400 SourceMeter is interfaced with the holder to perform galvanostatic charging. Charging currents are adjusted to ensure an effective rate of 1 C at the nanoscale contact area (i.e., electrode/electrolyte interface current density is 10 -50 A/cm 2). (The electrode/electrolyte interface current density is estimated from the contact area that we measure from the TEM image. 0.01 -0.05 μm 2). To facilitate nucleation, a steady bias of −2 V is applied, which is in line with the previously reported open-cell configurations.

Imaging
The dendrite growth is imaged in brightfield images in the range of 28,000×-115,000×. The total electron dose is kept below 50 e − /Å 2 /s to avoid beam effects. The blanking of the beam is also performed for the control experiments to verify the dendrite morphology does not change under electron beam irradiation. The dendrite growth duration for each deposition is 60 -180 s. The number of cells imaged is at least 12 for each independent experiment, to confirm reproducibility. This work involves three sessions between March and May 2024.

Data processing
The dendrite propagation velocity is calculated by frame-by-frame analysis of the growth front using ImageJ (v.1.54k). The kymograph analysis yields 5 -40 nm/s propagation velocities. Selected-area electron diffraction is used to characterize the structure of dendrite tips, which are single crystalline Li (body-centered cubic structure) with the growth direction along the ⟨111⟩ direction. The data is reported in terms of mean ± standard deviation among cells.

Methods

In situ TEM cell assembly. Open cell in situ TEM measurements were performed in a FEI Titan 80-300 environmental TEM with 300 kV operation and a Gatan OneView camera with continuous imaging mode at 25 fps. Lithium dendrite formation was monitored within a nanoscale electrochemical cell prepared inside a Hummingbird Scientific electrical biasing TEM holder. Half cell configuration was used with a ~100 nm thick Li 2 O-passivated Li metal electrode prepared via scratch of a metallic lithium foil (99.9%, Sigma Aldrich) with a tungsten wire (forming a native Li 2 O layer as a solid electrolyte). A sharp electrochemically polished copper wire counter-electrode was used (99.99%, Alfa Aesar, 250 µm diameter) and brought into contact with the Li 2 O surface via piezoerically controlled manipulation with sub-10 nm precision.

Electrochemical conditions. Galvanostatic charging was performed with a Keithley 2400 SourceMeter interfaced with the TEM holder. The charging currents were calibrated in order to provide effective 1 C charge rate in the nanoscale contact area (i.e., 10-50 A/cm 2 current densities at the electrode-electrolyte interface; the current density estimate was obtained using the contact area measured from the TEM images, 0.01-0.05 µm 2 ). In parallel, a constant negative bias of −2 V was applied to aid nucleation as in previous open cell setups.

Imaging. Dendrite formation was monitored in the bright field mode at magnifications of 28-115,000 ×. The total electron dose was kept below 50 e − /Å 2 /s to avoid beam effects. Beam-off control experiments showed that the morphology of dendrites is not affected by electron irradiation. Each dendrite deposition cycle lasted 60-180 s. At least 12 independent cells were imaged in three different experimental sessions (March-May 2024) to ensure reproducibility of the measurements.

Data analysis. Propagation velocity of dendrites was calculated from the frame-by-frame analysis of the propagation front in ImageJ (v.1.54k). Velocity of 5-40 nm/s was estimated from kymograph analysis. Dendrite tip structure was studied with selected area electron diffraction, showing single crystalline Li (body centered cubic) growth in ⟨111⟩ direction. Mean and standard deviation of the quantities are given for the different cells.

Limitations
Here we discuss limitations associated with our federated learning framework for the 12 participating hospital sites. First, despite our adoption of FedProx (μ=0.01) over vanilla FedAvg, the non-IID data heterogeneity between sites remained problematic. Pathology class imbalance (e.g., number of positive cases for pneumothorax) varied significantly among sites (e.g., Site 7, pediatric center in Lyon had less than 40 positive pneumothorax cases in 14 months of data collection, versus over 2100 cases from Site 3, a level 1 trauma center in Houston), which likely explains part of our best vs. worst site AUC performance difference of 6.8 (0.91 vs. 0.843) on the held out local test sets. Second, our harmonization preprocessing pipeline could not fully alleviate scanner/acquisition differences (e.g., 5/12 hospitals have GE Revolution CT scanner, the rest use Siemens SOMATOM/Canon Aquilion scanners), and there may still be residual domain shift related to reconstruction kernel and slice thickness that can't be fully accounted for by our histogram matching process. Third, we assume there's reliable communication and 48-hourly synchronous rounds for all 12 sites throughout the 9 months of training period (Jan.-Sept. 2025). However, we found that at least 3 sites had dropout at least once during a training round, necessitating resorting to stale client averaging which could bias against sites with more intermittent infrastructure. Fourth, while we did not share raw imaging data, we exchanged gradient updates without providing formal differential privacy guarantees, which could expose the data to possible membership inference/gradient inversion attacks (concern from 2 IRBs we work with, i.e., Houston and Lyon), but not sufficiently addressed in our current study. Fifth, we used held-out site-specific test set for evaluation, as opposed to a truly external cohort; so the generalizability of our framework to hospitals not in our 12-site consortium remains uncertain. We need to incorporate personalized federated learning (e.g., per-cluster/per-site adapters) and formal privacy metrics in our framework before we can consider clinical deployment.

Limitations

Here we mention several limitations to our federated learning framework at the 12 participating hospitals. First, we still face issues with non-IID data distribution across the hospitals, even with FedProx (μ=0.01) instead of vanilla FedAvg. The imbalance in pathology prevalence may vary greatly from one hospital to another, such as less than 40 positive cases of pneumothorax at Site 7 (a pediatric hospital in Lyon) over 14 months of data collection versus >2,100 positive cases at Site 3 (a level 1 trauma hospital in Houston), which potentially explains why we see an AUC difference of 6.8 between our best and worst performing hospital (0.91 vs. 0.843) on our held-out local test sets. Second, the scanner/acquisition harmonization pre-processing we used is not complete. 5 out of 12 hospitals utilized the GE Revolution CT scanner while the rest utilized different combinations of Siemens SOMATOM or Canon Aquilion scanners, and likely there is still residual domain shift from the reconstruction kernel and slice thickness not fully corrected by our histogram matching. Third, we assume perfect connectivity and a synchronized round of communication every 48 hours across 12 sites for a 9-month training period (Jan-Sep 2025). However, at least 3 sites dropped out for at least 1 round so we had to resort to stale-client averaging. This potentially adds more bias for sites with intermittent infrastructure. Fourth, despite not sharing actual imaging data, we exchanged the gradients without formal differential privacy guarantees. Potentially leading to membership inference or gradient inversion attacks, as pointed out by 2 of our IRBs (Houston and Lyon), but not fully addressed by the scope of this study. Fifth, instead of having an entirely external dataset, we evaluate on held-out test sets from each site. Thus, we do not yet validate the generalization to hospitals outside this 12-hospital consortium. We should consider the use of personalized federated learning (such as per-cluster/site adapters) and formal privacy accounting for these limitations before we can think about clinical deployment.

After the announcement on October 18, 2016 at Pleasanton, CA, 10x Genomics introduced the Chromium Single Cell Controller. The tool transformed single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) because of microfluidics droplets, gel beads with barcodes, and unique molecular identifiers. Thousands of cells could be easily analysed in parallel with the Chromium platform, which boosted the throughput greatly and made the analysis much more cost effective and time saving than previously used plate-based assays like Smart-seq2. The same period, during October 13-14, 2016 at Wellcome Trust, London, the Human Cell Atlas was announced to create a massive effort to define human cell types and states in tissues. [10x Genomics](https://s28.q4cdn.com/592666581/files/doc_news/2016/10/18/10x-genomics-announces-new-low-cost-single-cell-instrument.pdf), [Human Cell Atlas](https://www.humancellatlas.org/event/human-cell-atlas-launch-meeting/)

With the advancement of scRNA-seq, we can now analyse hundreds of thousands to millions of cells because of better droplet chemistries, sequencing strategies and computational tools. In addition, single nucleus RNA sequencing helps to analyse frozen or archived or difficult to dissociate intact and more complex tissues. The same period, transcriptome profiling can be combined with many other molecular features (e.g. chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, protein expression, immune receptor sequences) in parallel. These complementary technologies provide more accurate information for cell states, developmental processes, tumour heterogeneity, tissue specific regulation than the bulk RNA-seq approach. [Nature Reviews Genetics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-023-00580-2)

Recently spatial transcriptome profiling solves a major challenge in dissociative scRNA-seq, the loss of spatial information. The spatial analysis retains the positional information on transcript expression. Thus, it bridges the gap between molecular identities and tissue structure/cell interactions. High-throughput sequencing, multimodal analysis, spatial profiling, and advanced statistics or machine learning capabilities together turned scRNA-seq from a specialised measuring technique to a core technology to build cellular atlases and study diseases.

Results
Our ensemble of 5 ResNet-50 models had an average classification accuracy of 91.4% (on the held-out ISIC 2020 test data, n = 3,326 dermoscopic images), which exceeded the accuracy of any of the baseline models. The best model had an accuracy of 89.1%, whereas the worst had 86.7%, so our ensemble averaging improved accuracy by 2.3% compared to the best single model. For malignant melanoma detection, our ensemble's sensitivity was 88.9% (95% CI 86.4-91.1%), and specificity was 92.6% (95% CI 90.8-94.2%). Our ensemble had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.941, whereas individual models had AUROCs of 0.908-0.927.
Our misclassification analysis showed that 61.3% of the false negatives were cases that were ambiguous/low-contrast, as assessed by 2 board-certified dermatologists (blinded assessment, Cohen's κ 0.71), such as acral melanomas and high-pigmented nevi with regression elements. Our false positives were primarily seborrheic keratoses with inflammatory halo, and recurrent nevi, which represent common pitfalls in dermoscopic analysis.
Our class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis indicated that, for the correctly classified malignant cases, our ensemble focused on pigment network structures and atypical streaking in 78.4% of the cases. For the individual models, there was a higher tendency to focus on image artifacts such as ruler and gel bubbles (12.1% in Grad-CAM heatmaps vs. 4.6% for ensemble) which suggests that our ensemble helped in mitigating unnecessary dependence on spurious features.
Subgroup analysis by Fitzpatrick skin types showed no significant reduction in performance for skin types 4-6 (accuracy 90.2%, p = 0.18, DeLong test), although statistical power may be low due to the small sample size (n = 281). 5-fold cross-validation training on the ISIC 2020 training set of 26,604 images took ~14 hrs/fold using a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Our total time for training and inference was 96 hours. Performance for our ensemble was nearly, but not quite, as good as that of the consensus panel of 76 dermatologists (who had an accuracy of 92.8% on the same test set of n = 3,326, p = 0.06 on McNemar's test). Our results suggest that ResNet-50 ensembling is a powerful and dermatologist-level starting baseline for melanoma triage, but that our approach is still susceptible to diagnostically-ambiguous lesion morphologies.

In the misclassification analysis, 61.3% of the false-negative instances were from lesions that were rated as ambiguous/low contrast by two board-certified dermatologists (blinded review, Cohen's κ = 0.71), especially acral melanomas and heavily pigmented nevi with regression structures. Seborrheic keratoses with inflammatory halos and recurrent nevi are the main sources of false-positive instances, reflecting common pitfalls of dermoscopy.

The class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis showed that in 78.4% of malignant correctly classified instances, the ensemble focused on pigment network and atypical streaking, whereas individual models were found to more frequently fixate on artefacts, such as rulers and gel bubbles (12.1% in Grad-CAM heatmaps for individual models vs. 4.6% in the ensemble). This suggests that the ensembling helped reduce dependence on spurious features.

For subgroup analysis based on Fitzpatrick skin types, there was no statistically significant drop in performance for skin types IV-VI (90.2% accuracy, p = 0.18, DeLong test), but the number of instances (n = 281) is too small for a reliable conclusion. For 5-fold cross-validation training on the training dataset (26,604 images in the training split), the approximate time per fold was ~14 h on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. The ensemble's performance was close, but not better, to that of a consensus panel of 76 dermatologists (accuracy of 92.8% on the same test set, n = 3326, McNemar's test p = 0.06). Intranasal oxytocin: can a single dose improve trust? A placebo controlled study of trust in economic exchange and the role of prior social experience. Intranasal oxytocin has been suggested as a potential facilitator of trust in interpersonal relationships. But there is a mixed picture in the placebo-controlled studies to date. We studied the effect of a single dose of intranasal oxytocin on trust behavior in a game of economic exchange and the role of prior social experience.

180 healthy (94 females, 86 males, mean age 24.3 years, SD 4.1) adults sampled from the university community from March-November 2025, double-blind, placebo controlled, between-subjects design. Participants received 24 IU intranasal oxytocin (n=90) or placebo (n=90) 45 minutes prior to a multi-round trust game with an anonymous partner. Trust (measured as the % of endowment-10 money units each round, 12 rounds) transferred to counterpart (multiplied by 1.5 on return). Participants also completed an interpersonal trust scale, and a questionnaire about history of betrayals prior to drug administration.

Trust as measured by the % endowment transferred was significantly higher for participants given oxytocin (M=61.4%, SD=14.2) compared to placebo (M=52.7%, SD=15.8). t(178)=4.02, p<.001, Cohen's d=0.60. There was a significant interaction with betrayal history F(1,176)=9.87, p=.002. Trust increase % endowment transferred due to oxytocin was significant for those with low prior exposure to betrayal (Δ=12.9% points, p<.001) but not reliable for those with high exposure to betrayal (Δ=1.8% points, p=.41). No significant effects on amount returned (reciprocity) or on self reported dispositional trust scores. Thus the oxytocin manipulation appears to be changing risk-taking behaviour towards a particular partner and not general attitudes of trust.

Single-site laboratory data. Thus, there may be a role for oxytocin in facilitating decisions under uncertainty in the domain of trust, but this facilitation appears to be limited by individual social history. Replication with pharmacokinetic monitoring and other sample types should be considered prior to clinical or applied extrapolation.

Effects of intranasal oxytocin on trust - a placebo-controlled study

Intranasal oxytocin may boost the ability to trust in others. Results of placebo-controlled studies, however, are inconclusive. The goal of this study was to determine whether intranasal oxytocin, administered as a single dose, improves trusting behavior during an economic exchange game. Effects of intranasal oxytocin on trust were investigated in relation to previous social experience.

Double-blind placebo-controlled between-subjects study. One hundred eighty healthy adults, 94 women, 86 men, mean age 24.3 years, SD 4.1, drawn from a university community, March-November 2025, were randomly allocated to intranasal oxytocin, 24 IU (n=90), or placebo (n=90). This was administered 45 min prior to playing a multi-round trust game with an anonymous other. Trust was defined as proportion of an endowment sent (10 monetary units, each round. 12 rounds) to counterpart. Reciprocity was 1.5× returned. Participants filled in the Interpersonal Trust Scale and a questionnaire on betrayal history before drug administration.

Participants on oxytocin sent a higher proportion of their endowment (M=61.4%, SD=14.2) than those on placebo (M=52.7%, SD=15.8), t(178)=4.02, p<.001, Cohen's d=0.60. There was an interaction between betrayal history and the trust enhancing effect of oxytocin (F(1,176)=9.87, p=.002). Oxytocin increased sent proportion among those with low reported betrayal history (Δ=12.9 percentage points, p<.001) but not among those with high betrayal history (Δ=1.8 points, p=.41). Reciprocity (amount sent back by partners) was not affected significantly. Nor were dispositional trust scores (self-reports). This would mean that the oxytocin administration had a specific impact on the behavioral taking of risks with a certain other, not in general trust attitudes.

Data from one laboratory location indicates a possible role of oxytocin in promoting trust-related choices under uncertainty. Facilitation is restricted by individual social history. Results need to be replicated with PK-monitoring and in various samples before clinical/applied extrapolation can be attempted.

Near miss incident involving forklift and pedestrian in Warehouse B on February 8, 2026 around 2:15 PM. 3. Convex mirror at Aisle 4, Rack 12 corner not present since Jan reconfiguration

The area of concern was especially apparent between March 10 and March 24 where multiple customers communicated delays of 3-7 business days. The complaints were primarily centered around orders heading to New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Pennsylvania. Additionally, some customers have communicated that the estimated delivery date changes after they have checked out without the company proactively communicating this.

Outside of these issues, the next biggest categories of complaint tickets were related to packages arriving damaged, wrong items received, billing questions, and delivery address issues (37 total complaints). While these are all smaller categories, the ones related to the Newark delays are the biggest risk to customer satisfaction as they're concentrated in a region and lead to repeat communications.

Customer Support has started tagging tickets related to Newark separately and has started escalating delayed shipments to Logistics each afternoon. Logistics is currently assessing staffing, carrier pickup times, and package processing capability at the Newark hub. Customer Support representatives are also doing a better job at communicating the reason for the delay to customers and setting expectations around the next tracking update.

Going forward for April - key focuses should be:
- Implement a daily Newark delay dashboard
- Proactively communicate to customers when shipments are stagnant for more than 48 hours
- Have a weekly review with primary carrier around hub performance
- Reassess progress on April 15 and at month end. Looking to get Newark related complaints to under 25% of total monthly tickets.

6 months in - iPhone 15 Pro still the best phone I've had, but... 
 Battery life is good, not great.  Average day (say, 4 hours of screen time, mix of slack/spotify/camera work).  I'm usually sitting at 20-25% by 9pm.  (if i unplug at 7am).  More intense days (say, using the nav system on road trip to Lake Tahoe in March, or video-recording at a friend's wedding in June) I can be down to single digits by early evening. 
 
 Feels like Apple's 80% threshold for health after 500 cycles is accurate.  I'm still at 91% according to settings, and haven't really noticed a significant degradation.  I overnight charge with a 20W USB-C (brick).  I'll top off via magsafe at my desk.  Wireless charging takes significantly longer, and is hotter, so I try to avoid it unless I'm in a hurry. 
 
 Biggest difference (from my previous 13 Pro): camera!  48mp main sensor lets me take legitimately printable shots (blown up a couple to 11x14" for a gallery wall.  no obvious softness). 
 3x telephoto (77mm equivalent) is the one I use most.  Great for candid shots in a restaurant where it might be weird to get closer. 
 Low light improvement.  A dimly lit bar in downtown Austin (April), was able to take reasonably good (and not too noisy) photos without a tripod. 
 
 Only complaint: Night mode seems to want 2-3 seconds longer to find focus than I'd prefer.  Sometimes in portrait mode it'll blur the details on a set of earrings that it shouldn't. 
 
 $999 for 128gb model is expensive, but I'd do it again.  Titanium body (has survived a couple drops so far) and the camera (which has replaced my previously-separate point+shoot camera).

review_product_02_luna.text:
Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer (2023) is an epic and very intense film. It really comes into its own when viewed in IMAX as the sheer scale of the experience when seeing the Trinity test is overwhelming. The build-up to the explosion, the flash and the delayed sound of the explosion are genuinely intimidating rather than just being a spectacle. The score by Ludwig Göransson and the thunderous sound design compliment the film without it being a standard action film. 
 The performances are amazing and are led by a wonderful Cillian Murphy as J. Robert Oppenheimer. He shows Oppenheimer to be a genius, vain, neurotic and increasingly tortured by what he has done. The supporting cast is fantastic. Robert Downey Jr. is great as Lewis Strauss. Emily Blunt as Kitty Oppenheimer and Matt Damon as General Leslie Groves are also very good. While at first it seems confusing and complicated with multiple timelines and black and white segments it gradually coheres and paints a fascinating picture of the interplay of science with politics, ego and fear. 
 This is a very long film. At 3 hours it's a long sit. There are a few scenes in the court and security hearings which can drag a bit and require you to pay close attention to what can be dense dialog. Ultimately though, the length makes sense as it's not just telling the story of the Manhattan Project. It's telling that story, the personal story of Oppenheimer and the political aftermath of it all over a period of decades. In IMAX the detail and scale helps make it easier to swallow. But perhaps have a break first as it's not a lazy history lesson. It's a fascinating and tiring film. You won't forget it easily.

Chris Nolan's Oppenheimer (2023) is a deeply compelling and intense film. Especially in IMAX. The scale is so overwhelming that the Trinity test part is absolutely terrifying, the silence before the blast, the flash, the slight delay until the roar that shakes your insides. It's more than a spectacle. Ludwig Gorensson's score and the pounding sound design add to the experience but don't make it feel like an action film.

Cillian Murphy is simply amazing as J. Robert Oppenheimer. He's brilliant, full of self-love, nervous, and being tormented by the aftermath. Not to mention the supporting cast. In particular Robert Downey Jr (Lewis Strauss), Emily Blunt (Kitty Oppenheimer) and Matt Damon (Gen. Leslie Groves). The jumping of times and the black and white sequences are confusing at first but slowly it starts to paint a very interesting story of how science mixed with politics, self-love and fear.

Oppenheimer is 3 hours long, no doubt about it. Certain court sequences and the security hearings are slow and the dialogue is so dense, you really need to pay attention. But it feels largely acceptable for the fact that it covers the manhattan project, Oppenheimer's life and the political aftermath over decades. It's easier to digest in IMAX since the scale and the details are larger. You probably want to have a break before-hand. This isn't a casual historical piece. It's a very absorbing but also tiring piece of work. You feel its weight long after the movie has ended.

200 hours later. Finally. And now I'm ready to say this. 
 In summary, Baldur's gate 3 is one of the best RPGS I have ever played. And sometimes, it's one of the most infuriating ones. 
 I'm gonna start with the bugs. Because there are a lot of bugs. I've seen a lot of them through my honor mode run (rip, 140 hours, shadowheart pathing bug made her go off a cliff in shar temple). Characters going through walls in Grymforge, to my honour (RIP), Karlach sometimes cutting her sentences off mid way. Act 3 infamous performance drops that make my 3080ti go to 25fps in lower city. Once upon a time, Laezel refused to follow me for an entire session. I had to fast travel to break her loose. Patch 5 fixed a lot, but even now, 6 months after August 2023 launch. I still stumble upon the occasional broken quest flags. Dame Aylin was hovering around outside my camp for 3 ingame days last week. 
 But none of it kept me from starting my 4th playthrough. Because my god the replay value is insane. First playthrough was the good guy paladin. 2nd playthrough was Dark Urge bard romancing Astarion (10/10, no notes). 3rd playthrough was an evil drow run that had a totally different Act 2 experience. The origin characters are so well written. Now I'm on Karlach origin run, just to get her perspective. There is so much to see in act 3 that I found whole quest lines I missed on my first and second playthrough. The circus of last light. House of hope. Mizora whole thing. 
 
 Is it perfect? No. 
 Act 3 is still jankier than Act 1 & 2. Epilogue slides feels rushed in comparison to the rest of the game. 
 But 200 hours, 4 characters. And I'm still seeing new dialogue, new outcomes. New ways to solve problems. The day I rolled nat 20 to talk down boss instead of fight him, I understood Larian's creation. 
 
 Recommended. Obviously. But save often.

review_product_08_luna.text:
Spider-man: Across the Spider-Verse is what you get when the animation stops being a vessel and becomes the nervous system of the story. Every shot is like its been handpainted, coded or cross-universe extracted at 24fps.

Its one thing to see Miles Morales move in Brooklyn in a completely different way than Gwen Stacy’s painted watercolor world where color runs, and emotions literally change the world. It’s another thing to dive into Mumbattan and its eye-opening blend of neon, comic book panels, indian architecture, train race sequences. The Spider Society office is a literal animation style museum. Hundreds of spider-people and how they all move with their own weird physics, shapes, visual code.

I really enjoyed the film’s use of visual language to drive emotion. How Gwen’s room around her changes when she’s having this fight with her dad. You don’t need to have a whole page of text. Miguel O’hara’s body changes, stretches and snaps like a bad graphic novel illustration of someone getting angry. The spot evolves from this silly white black pimple thing to actually being a horror nightmare. Like it’s erasing the world around him.

This movie from 2/6/2023 has the visual bravado of experimental film. But it’s also a blockbuster. Its maximalism and chaos and beauty. It finds new ways of making movement matter. I can freeze pretty much any shot and put it on a wall. But the real magic is watching them smash, change and race to the impossible.

'Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse' is what happens when animation ceases to simply be the receptacle for a story and instead becomes its nervous system. Everything feels hand-painted, slapped together or imported from another universe (24 frames per second).

Miles Morales swinging through Brooklyn has a different sense of tempo compared to Gwen Stacy's watercolored universe with bleeding colors and emotions literally influencing the background. We then shift gears into Mumbattan - a spectacular mixing pot of neon, comic book panels, Indian architectural styles and dynamic train chases. The Spider Society building itself is a museum of animation styles. The numerous Spider-People are moving around and have their own weird physics, silhouettes, style.

The movie often lets the images be the emotional carrier. The way Gwen's room shifts and changes around her during her clash with her father is more powerful than words on the page. The way Miguel O'Hara's body stretches and snaps feels like an angry graphic novel doodle. The evolution of the Spot from a silly white and black zit to a deeply scary presence as though the movie is being wiped away around him.

It's a blockbuster movie with the aesthetic ambitions of experimental filmmaking. Maximalist, chaotic, beautiful and always finding new ways to make motion express something. I could grab almost every frame and put it up on the wall. But the real magic is seeing them crash and morph and rush towards the impossible.

June 2, 2023 release.
